messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.body_plain:
Bob - Thanks for the note.

The use case is for online change point detection over time. My assumption is that the underlying generation process would jump from one state to another (and the jump is “big" compared to observation error)

At time=t, I have new observation y[n] and old data y[1:n-1] and I want to know the probability of y[n] is generated from a state that is different from that had generated y[1..n-1].

Intuitively, I thought of fitting a change point model to y[1.. n] and check for existence of change point around n. Perhaps, there are better ways?

Thanks,

Andy

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.body_plain:
There are times when we fit unrelated models, or we have models coming from different sources, and predictive model comparison is one way to evaluate these.  Especially the new form where we get the contribution of loo (or waic) for each data point.

But if you have a model (in this case, the change-point model in which the size of the change is an unknown parameter) which includes the smaller model (in this case, the no-change-point model, which is theta=0) as a special case, i’d rather just fit the big model.  If you want to say, hey, let’s use the smaller model because it’s simpler and easier to work with, then, sure, I do think that loo or waic can be a way to make this decision.  But I definitely wouldn’t frame it as “To determine if the time series has a change-point or not.”  The time series, whatever it is, has a change point at every time.  The question might be, “Is a change point necessary to model these data?”  That’s a question I could get behind.

Does this help?
A

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, September 1, 2015 at 7:42:59 AM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Is it possible to run stan and then read the results directly from disk?  I have encounter memory
> problems for large panel data sets and large number of parameters.

In addition to the specific problem of not having enough memory there are a few long-standing issues with R/Rcpp/rstan and memory (I'm sure they'll get fixed someday but they're not straightforward).  For the moment I think the best practice for when you really need to save all those parameters is to use CmdStan to run the model, generate the giant .csv file by saving all the parameters, and then deal with processing a giant .csv file.  I think after the output refactor becomes part of the main branch it'll be easier to resolve these issues but until then... CmdStan is better than rstan at chugging its way through giant data sets.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.body_plain:
There's a change-point example in the manual in the chapter
on latent discrete parameters.

I'm not sure if Andrew approves of the discrete coding or
would rather an explicit prior on a continuous cut point and
then a discretization that puts the prior probability of
being in an interval between two measurements as the difference
of CDFs for the continous prior.  It wouldn't be too hard to add
that, but it's a lot of CDF computation, which isn't very efficient.

- Bob

I think lambda is OK as is, but kappa isn't --- it
should have upper=100 to match this:

>   real<lower=0> kappa;

>   kappa ~ uniform(0,100); ## Dispersion parameter of NB

I don't understand why the magic number 1e-5 is there (nor
do I understand the "0" in "1e-05" --- I didn't even think it
was legal to start a number with "0"):

> Y[t] ~ neg_binomial_2(lambda[t]+1e-05,kappa);

I'd think the bigger issue would be with kappa being near zero.
So I think you need to go into the model and instrument with print()
statements to see where things are diverging.  Or define generated
quantities like

> numReleased*psi*exp(-alpha*(exp(beta*t)-1)/beta)

to see what's happening to the values.

The inner plus outer exponential form is tricky, because the psi,
alpha, and beta are going to wind up highly correlated in the
posterior.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
What I was trying to convey is that the model should have
support for all parameter values satisfying the declared constraints.

I believe in this case, Andrew's recommending an overdispersion variable only
constrained to be positive

  real<lower=0> kappa;

But if this is all you did, you'd get an improper uniform, so to
satisfy the "no uniform priors!" dictum, you need a prior

  kappa ~ ...;

But I don't know which one Andrew would suggest for overdispersion in
neg_binomial_2.  Andrew, your Wiki awaits:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

And just to clarify, Andrew, should we get rid of all uniform priors in
the manual, even the unconstrained ones, or is it just the interval constraint
you object to?  That is, should we not have regressions with
improper uniform priors on coefficients and scale as examples?

As is, we have quite a few models in our examples repo that use these
uniform priors constrained to an interval.  We can prioritize updating
those if we can deprioritize something else.  Or find a volunteer willing
to go through them.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
For understanding HMC, start with Radford Neal's paper in the MCMC
Handbook (it's a free sample chapter online).  Then maybe go to
something like Michael's paper on hierarchical modeling on arXiv.

But the issue isn't HMC or Gibbs or Metropolis per se, but the interaction
of those algorithms and step sizes with floating point arithmetic.

The point is that you want to figure out where you get overflow
or underflow in the exploration of the posterior.  This often happens when
parameters get pushed near boundaries.  Parameters constrained to be in (0, 1)
can underflow to 0 or overflow to 1, for example.

You could do worse than reading the Wikipedia:

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_point

Beyond that, I wouldn't mind getting a good recommendation for
a numerical analysis book myself.

It'll also be a problem if your model's not identified.  You could start
with the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual.

- Bob

Hello all,

Thank you for your suggestions.

Whilst your points generally focus on the dispersion parameter, I would say that even for the Poisson model I get the same results (here I have included the perhaps simpler Weibull mortality) below. I also attach a scatter plot of samples from the posterior (although to be clear here, since I have divergent iterations, it isn't really the posterior, but this result comes up from simulations of fake data as well, where there are no divergent iterations), and we see that beta and mu are highly correlated. Any ideas?

Best,

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.body_plain:
I never understand specifically what's Andrew's suggesting.
I think the takeaway on model-non-comparison was this:

  if you have a model (in this case, the change-point model in
  which the size of the change is an unknown parameter) which
  includes the smaller model (in this case, the no-change-point
  model, which is theta=0) as a special case, i’d rather just fit
  the big model.

My guess is that he has a whole suite of models of varying
granularity in mind.  Because he goes on to say

  The time series, whatever it is, has a change point at every time.

This implies to me that Andrew wants to unask the question of
whether the sequence has 0, 1, or T-1 change points?  By definition
the sequence has T-1 observations. So it's just a question of what you want
to model.

But it's not a simple modeling change.

The no change-point model is easy

   for (t in 1:T)
     y[t] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Pardon the non-vectorization --- it's just trying to make it unambiguous
there's a single mu and sigma and T different y.

Allowing one change point you need to marginalize out as
in the manual.  Then it's a question of how you model where
the change occurs --- for a proper prior on a latent continuous
change point, you need the CDF differences (for same reason
as in our last discussion here on CDF diffs for rounding).  Or you
can just hack it up as uniform as I did in the example in the manual
where the times are evenly spaced.

But when you allow T-1 change points, all of a sudden you're back
to something like the first model, with a time series

  for (t in 1:T)
   y[t] ~ normal(mu[t], sigma);

Assuming no stochastic volatility (i.e., a fixed sigma).  Then you
need a prior for mu, probably one based on autoregression.

At least I think that's what's going on here.

- Bob

> On Sep 2, 2015, at 1:16 AM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> In terms of coding, Andrew's proposed model should actually be easier in some sense, as it doesnt require marginalizing any discrete parameters. Change points at all time periods is equivalent to letting the relevant parameter vary over time, which for Stan usually just means declaring the parameter as a vector of length T and using a loop or a vectorized equivalent to estimate all T of the parameters (which can have a hierarchical prior if appropriate or independent priors).
>

messages.body_plain:
I think that makes is more obvious where the confusion is. I think there are those people who when asking the question "Where is the change point?" want a decision between

There is a change point at s and its size (difference between e, l) is such.
OR
There is not enough evidence for a change point anywhere

And then there are people who want an answer to

Suppose there is a change point, where could it be and what would its size be?

The answer to the last question could of course be: there is very little evidence for a very small change point here, which is unsatisfying for NHST-trained people, who want to know if it's signifiant or not.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
messages.body_plain:
Anyone care to comment on this possible prior for the effects of a K-level ordinal input variable? The idea is that you use a Dirichlet distribution for partitioning the range from beta[1] to beta[K], and you use an independent prior on the magnitude of that range.

    beta[1] <- -scale;
    beta[K] <- scale;
    // Now make beta[k + 1] - beta[k] be fraction p[k] of (beta[K] - beta[1])
    range <- beta[K] - beta[1];
    b <- beta[1];
    for (k = 1; k + 1 < K; ++k)
        beta[k + 1] <- beta[k] + p[k] * range;

    scale ~ normal(0, sigma);
    p ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K-1));

Larger values for alpha give a larger preference for equally-spaced betas.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change point detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi, there are 2 issues here.

First is the distribution of change points over time.  As Bob notes, I prefer to avoid change points entirely as I think that every moment has its own changes.  Something that looks roughly like discrete change points can be constructed using continuous change points with a long tailed distribution of the amount of change.

The second issue is, if we do have a model with a discrete change point at just one time, to avoid the question, “Is there a change point?” by saying that there definitely _is_ a change point of unknown magnitude.

It was the second point that I was trying to make in my response to that earlier question.  I think of this second model as a bit of a compromise.  Yes, it assumes a particular change point.  But it is still a continuous-parameter model, and I like that.

A

messages.subject: On uniform priors
messages.subject_clean: On uniform priors
messages.body_plain:
Hi, yes, I agree with Bob that if you really have a constrained prior on a parameter, it makes sense to define it on a constrained space.  But I really don’t like these uniform(0,A) priors.  If you want to constrain a parameter to be less than 100, say, it’s my guess that you really think your parameter is less than 10, and maybe something like an exponential(.1) prior would do the job.

Unconstrained uniforms (i.e., in Stan, not putting in a prior at all) are another story.  They’re wrong too, of course, but they’re not pretending to be anything they’re not.  If you don’t put in a prior, it’s understood that you are ready to put in a real prior later, if necessary.

A

messages.subject: Re: Conditional Logistic Regression in Stan?
messages.subject_clean: Conditional Logistic Regression in Stan?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks!

Has anyone successfully implemented conditional logistic regression in Stan since this last posting?  I have implemented the methods employed in the attached paper using clogit{survival} in R for a variety of resource selection models, but I would love to give it a go in Stan.  Before trying to brute force my way through the process (as an ecologist and not a statistician), I figured I'd check to see if anyone had example code they would be willing to share...so as not to reinvent the wheel so to speak.  Thanks for any help!

Cheers,
Peter

On Saturday, June 22, 2013 at 1:31:21 PM UTC-6, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, June 22, 2013 2:59:21 PM UTC-4, Noah wrote:
> > A few questions related to a conditional logistic regression.
> >
> > 1) Is there a way in Stan to model a conditional logistic regression?  (I didn't see it in the manual)
>
> I think Stan can do pretty much any regression, but the conditional logistic log-likelihood isn't programmed into Stan yet, so the log-likelihood would have to be evaluated using Stan code and manipulation of the lp__ symbol.
>
> > 2) With a CLR, the posterior is a probability estimate of the outcome for each member of a group, with the within-group probabilities summing to 1.  With many draws from the posterior, I will effectively have many draws of possible probabilities. (I have N draws of probabilities for K members of a race.)  How would I then simulate outcomes?  What is the probability of member i winning?
>
> There is a good explanation of the probabilities and the likelihood here
>
> http://www.stata.com/support/faqs/statistics/within-group-collinearity-and-clogit/
>
> To implement this in Stan, you will need to take logs to get the categorical log-likelihood and you probably want to use some of the log_sum_exp() tricks to prevent numerical overflow. In any event, once you get the posterior probabilities, you can just draw from categorical_rng() for each group.
>
> > 3) I have probabilities of winning for each race member (from another model.)  It would be interesting to treat those as priors for a model in Stan.  However, I'm used to thinking about priors on the coefficients as drawn from some distribution, not actual point estimates of the outcomes.  How would I set that up in Stan?
>
> Does your model have predictors? If so, it is going to be pretty tedious to analytically derive the distribution of the coefficients conditional on the probability of winning. In Stan, you proceed numerically by adjusting lp__ by the log absolute Jacobian determinant of the transformation from probabilities to coefficients, but this is difficult at best.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: New papers on LOO/WAIC and Stan
messages.body_plain:
The difference between lppd_i and loo_i has been used as a sensitivity measure
(see, e.g., Gelfand et al 1992). Pareto shape parameter estimate k is likely to
be large if the difference between lppd_i and loo_i is large. It's not yet
clear to me whether the Pareto shape parameter estimate k would be better than
lppd_i-loo_i, but at least we know that estimate for lppd_i-loo_i is too small
if k is close to 1 or larger, so it might be better to look at k.

In stack example with normal model, k for one observation is large, but with
student-t model k is smaller. Normal model is same as student-t model, but with
very strong prior on degrees of freedom. So it's not just about having strong
prior or more shrinkage, but having a model which can describe the observations
well. With increased shrinkage and non-robust observation model, the one
observation could still be surprising.

Naturally it's not always the best solution to change to a more robust
observation model allowing "outliers". Instead it might be better to make the
regression function more nonlinear (that is having a less strong prior), or
transform covariates, or add more covariates.

So I do recommend looking at Pareto shape parameter values, but I don't
recommend to increase shrinkage if the values are large.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
I'm running Stan via R, with a single core. (This is just for testing for now.)

I have a model that ran in about an hour with the R command;
stan(file='fit_SIS_Generic.stan', data=data_trial,iter=100, chains=1, seed=194838, refresh=20)

(I am aware that this is too few iterations, etc. Again, this was for testing.)

I changed that slightly, to
stan(file='fit_SIS_Generic.stan', data=data_trial, iter=100, chains=2, seed=194838, refresh=20),

and the first chain took about 5 times as long, per the updates delivered (the second chain was still running and I killed it after a dozen hours.)

There are other problems with the model, but I was surprised to see that running chains=2, where they run in sequence, not in parallel, should affect the timing - especially given the indetical random seed, which I would think gives the same process and results, though this may not be true when running multiple chains.

I looked at the manual, and the only thing I could find was that there were differences that could occur in how the model runs due to thread safety for multiple chains.

Is there a different / better explanation?

messages.subject: expensive, numerical posterior
messages.subject_clean: expensive, numerical posterior
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is more of a conceptual question, instead of asking for advice on a
specific model/Stan feature, but I hope I could get some help or
suggestions here; as I want to use Stan for something I have not seen it
used for so I don't know whether my plans are feasible or even make
sense.

I have an economic model for which the likelihood/posterior p(theta|y)
is

1. expensive to calculate (takes about 15s on a reasonably good
computer for a single point),

2. is only available through a numerical algorithm (the economic model
needs to be solved for the law of motion), so there is no derivative
information and I cannot code it in Stan.

Traditionally in economics RMW (Random Walk Metropolis) is suggested for
these problems, but I was wondering if I could somehow leverage the
algorithms of Stan for it, for more efficient sampling.

I was thinking about the following:

a. obtain an approximation q(theta|y) to p in a representation that Stan
can calculate efficiently,

b. use rejection sampling for the result to obtain samples from p.

Reading the approximation: looking at the literature the algorithm
suggested is a normal approximation around some mode. But the problem
seems to be severely multimodal and I doubt that this would be efficient.

I think I can obtain a state-space form, extending with unobserved state
x and make it a Kalman filter where matrices depend on theta, for which
I would use a linear, Pade or a global approximation then marginalize.

But I am not clear on where the approximation should be "good": ideally
it would be best on the region where most of the posterior is, but then
I only know that once I do the rejection sampling. Would it then make
sense to iterate (find another approximation knowing the posterior,
etc)?

Suggestions, pointers to the literature, etc, would be very
welcome. Sorry if the question is vague.

Best,

Tamas

messages.body_plain:
No, no, no, no!

The problem with these kinds of approximations (often called emulators
in the literature) is that interpolations in high dimensions are ill-posed —
there are a huge number of possible interpolations and only a singular
few are actually consistent with the truth.  So what happens in practice
is you try to interpolate your few numerical evaluations but most of the
resulting proposals fail.

What you really want to do is open up the black box of your economic
model.  Go back to the diff eqs, for example, and figure out the gradients
from there and run HMC.  You can already see that we’re starting to
do this with explicit ODE models, but you’ll just have to figure out what
those ODEs are.  Yes, those gradients can be expensive but the sampling
speed up you get over something like RWM is huge and makes it all
the worth while.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] expensive, numerical posterior
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] expensive, numerical posterior
messages.body_plain:
> The problem is that most economic models are forward-looking and solving
> for the coefficients of the ODEs is the nontrivial step, imposed by
> equilibrium conditions, usually done by iterative numerical methods. I
> don't think one can code that in Stan, but I will look into it.

There are two ways of using these models.  One is to code up the solver
in Stan and let Stan automatically differentiate through the solver.  This
works but tends to be slow.  Another is to differentiate the original system
and then figure out how to solve for those derivatives.  We do this
automatically for ODEs in Stan, but can be done analytically for all kinds
of systems such as implicit constraints that require root solvers.

> On the other hand, I think can provide a linear approximation to the
> model, and then an approximation of the parameters of that as a function
> of the model parameters, which I believe is good or at least OK.

Then go ahead and try it.  But keep in mind that for anything but really simple
models (which wouldn’t then require such complex solvers) these approximations
fail hard pretty quickly.

These are not easy problems — but if your likelihood is a black box
then there’s only much you can do to explore it efficiently.  You _have_
to open that box, which is usually a good idea for reproducible science
anyways.

messages.body_plain:
My experience with redirecting output of parallel chains to text file was rather satisfactory.  I have used the following code (chain output was redirected to outfile so I was able to follow the progress of all chains):

par.stan <- function (file, code, data, warmup, n.draws, chains, pars,
init, outfile)
{
# compile C++ code
sm <- stan (file = file, model_code = code, data = data, chains = 1,
iter = 0)
CL <- makeCluster (chains, outfile = outfile)
clusterExport (cl = CL, c ("data", "pars", "n.draws", "warmup", "init"))
sflist <- parLapply (CL, 1 : chains, fun = function (cid) {
require (rstan)
if (length (init) == 1) {
if (init == "random") {
init <- "random"
} else {
init <- list (init [[cid]])
}
} else {
init <- list (init [[cid]])
}
stan (fit = sm, data = data, chains = 1, warmup = warmup,
iter = n.draws + warmup, pars = pars, init = init,
chain_id = cid)
})
stopCluster (CL)
if (chains == 1) {
return (sflist [[1]])
} else {
return (sflist2stanfit (sflist))
}
}

Thank you,
Linas

Back to the original question: David, is your computer swapping? Do you get the same slowdown using CmdStan?

I suspect that the posterior for the Stan program you've written is ill-behaved and that might be causing your problems:
- how reasonable are your results? do they differ run to run? are there divergent iterations? are you hitting the tree depth limit?
- can you try adding stronger priors to see if that will help?
- I would suggest trying to run more warmup iterations. Perhaps the adaptation parameters are not being tuned anywhere reasonably.
- is the model non-identifiable?

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan team,

I'd like first to thank you all for the amazing work done with Stan. Special kudos for ShinyStan which is truly awesome!

I have a question I haven't been able to find an answer for. I fitted a relatively simple hierarchical model (no intercept, modeled slopes), everything went smoothly, except that obviously one of the four chains I used encountered some autocorrelation problems (see below).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-yP67SGLUKSM/VevSrfVpl0I/AAAAAAAAXyk/cvOFXds2jz4/s1600/Capture%2Bdu%2B2015-09-06%2B07%253A39%253A41.png>
Now of course I could refit entirely the model with maybe more burnin samples. But since only one of the chains seems to have a problem, I was wondering whether there is an easy way to disgard that chain and possibly replace it with another one? Does it make sense or is there a problem with this approach I'm failing to see (I'm pretty much a n00b when it comes to serious Bayesian modeling)?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Throw or replace one chain?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Throw or replace one chain?
messages.body_plain:
> But since only one of the chains seems to have a problem, I was wondering whether there is an easy way to disgard that chain and possibly replace it with another one?

Nope.  Never.  Nada.

Markov chains are valid only when they are well-behaved from any starting point
Even one chain misbehaving diagnoses pathologies that affect the others — basically
there may be a pathology region of parameter space but only one chain was lucky
enough to find it.  The more chains the more likely you are to identify such pathologies,
which is why we recommend running as many chains as you can.

messages.body_plain:
If you’re running with multiple chains then the seed gets incremented for
each chain to ensure that they don’t all give the same results (i.e. the
RNG will be independent for each chain).  Consequently when running
multiple chains you should not expect the same exact results, and
one chain can easily get stuck in a pathological region if your model
is ill-posed.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Massive slowdown from setting threads=2 (not 1)?
messages.body_plain:
It is perhaps possible that the threads are executed out of order, i.e. the second one first. If there are multiple chains and a specified seeds, Stan winds the PRNG forward by some fraction of its period depending on the chain_id. This ensures that you are not using the same random numbers across multiple chains but it would also mean you can get very different behavior across chains.

Ben

Thanks for the reply.
I have tried rescaling some of my data so that the coefficients are all of magnitude 1 and have tried some more informative priors for alpha and tau but I am still finding it struggles to converge and the neff values are very small (<10) even when using 100000 iterations.
Any other clues as to what could be the problem? This is my code now (I have also rewritten the spline terms inside the stan code):

X <- cbind(Intercept=1, dat$h1n1_rate_ILI, dat$h3n2_rate_ILI, dat$ph1n1_rate_ILI, dat$ph1n1_rate_ILI_Pandemic, dat$B_rate_ILI, dat$RSV_rate_ILI, dat$TEMP, dat$TEMP2, dat$TEMP3, dat$AH, dat$AH2, dat$AH3, dat$NameChange)

N <- dim(X)[1]

k <- dim(X)[2]

DeathRate <- dat$DeathRate

WeekIndex <- dat$week.index

H <- 30 #no. of knots

xi <- seq(1,761, 761/30)

data <- list(N=N, X=X, k=k, DeathRate=DeathRate, WeekIndex=WeekIndex, H=H, xi=xi)

stan_code<-"

data {

    int<lower=0> N; //no. of weeks

    int<lower=0> k; //no. of predictors

    real DeathRate[N]; //outcome

    matrix[N, k] X; //predictor matrix

    vector[N] WeekIndex; // vector for spline function

    int<lower=0> H;

    vector[H] xi;

    }

transformed data {

    matrix[N, H+4] week_s;

    matrix[N, k+H+4] Z;

    for(n in 1:N) {

        week_s[n,1] <- WeekIndex[n]^0;

        week_s[n,2] <- WeekIndex[n]^1;

        week_s[n,3] <- WeekIndex[n]^2;

        week_s[n,4] <- WeekIndex[n]^3;

        for(h in 1:H)

        week_s[n,h+4] <- fmax(0,(WeekIndex[n] - xi[h])^3);

    }

    Z <- append_col(X, week_s);

  }

parameters {

vector[k+H+4] alpha;

real <lower=0> taud;

}

model {

    vector[N] mud;

    mud <- Z*alpha;

    alpha ~ normal(0,10);

  taud ~ cauchy(0,5);

DeathRate ~ normal(mud, taud);

}"

Thanks in advance!

Ah. It's making sense now. I don't know if there's a better way to form that error message.

Stan is an imperative language (it executes things in the order you write it).

If you look at the transformed data block:
transformed data{
  int<lower=1> N;
  row_vector[D] x[N];
  matrix [N,D] x_mat;
  vector[N] mu;
  N<- N_obs + N_pred;
  ...

you are trying to declare x as: row_vector[D] x[N]. Here, N is still 0. It only gets set to N_obs + N_pred after x is declared.

One way to fix it is to declare x as:
  row_vector[D] x[N_obs + N_pred];

With that fix, you'll run into problems for x_mat and mu, but I'll let you take care of that.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Sorry for bumping an old thread. I was not sure if I should make a new thread or not, so I just used this.

Anyway, in continuation of the discussion on mixture models, I was considering if it was possible to discard the principle of exchangeability.

In the standard model, the features are exchangeable and independant:

p(y|theta, mu, sigma) = \sigma_i^K theta_i * N(y|mu_k, sigma_k)

But would it be possible to make the current feature dependant on the N last? Written in very poor math,

p(y|theta, mu, sigma, y_{t-1}) = \sigma_i^K theta_i * N(y|y_{t-1}, mu_k, sigma_k)

I found one article expanding the LDA model with a first order Markov property for the sequence of words (https://labs.yahoo.com/_c/uploads/ECMLPKDD2013MLJ.pdf). This model is, however, slightly different in that it assumes discrete features coming from a multinomial distribution with a parameter depending on the previous word. I am not sure how this translates into Gaussian distributions.

I tried creating a very simple model, where I just add the previous observation (https://gist.github.com/demodw/b07a2eb962898e8703da). In Stan code,

log(theta[k]) + normal_log(y[n, m] + y[n, m-1], mu[k], sigma[k])

But I am not sure if that even makes sense. I guess my biggest problem is I find it difficult to formulate the likelihood function mathematically.

Thanks in advance.

David

> > > > Yes, exactly. Except y[n] is is not the count of the places, but the count of the number of proteins in a particular place. In figure 1a from the paper, there are 60 such places. In each of the 60 places, there are either 0 proteins (the protein is not found in the given place or could not be detected), or a number in the billions if the protein is present. Each y[n] thus holds a vector of counts for the given place, so that y[n,m] is the count of protein n in place m.
> > >
> > > Thanks --- that's what I was trying to say.  I can't see
> > > the paper (and please don't send a pirated copy to our list).
> > >
> > > > What we want to identify are the proteins that has the same profile / is drawn from the same mixture. If two proteins are co-migrating, they are most likely physically interacting in a complex. At least that is what we hypothesise. The idea running the Bayesian model would be to have priors on the number of mixtures, as well as infer which proteins are co-migrating. It could be there are better ways of doing it, but our initial thought was the Bayesian framework as it is quite flexible.
> > >
> > > Thanks --- now I get it.

> > > you use for the mixture,

> > > log Pr[n in cluster k | y, theta, mu, sigma]
> > >
> > >    = ps[k] - log_sum_exp(ps)
> > >
> > > For example, when you do log_sum_exp(ps), that's the unnormalized log
> > > probabilities, so you need to divide each of the ps[iby the sum, which is another
> > > so you just need to do
> > >
> > >
> >
> > I think it somehow truncated this part, but I am assuming you are referring to the softmax function, yes?
>
> I probably just forgot to finish it.  You probably don't need
> all of softmax, which computes this value for each k.
>
> > >
> > > Then calculate
> > >
> > > Pr[n and m in same cluster | y]

> > >

> > Sometimes I forget the basics, especially when working in these higher-level frameworks. This is very close to what we are trying to infer. However, If we calculated the probability of two proteins coming from the same complex, how would we combine this information to assign multiple memberships per protein?
>
> The model implicitly assumes every protein comes from a single
> mixture component.  If you want to relax this, you need to go to

To move to an AR(1)-like structure (see the manual sections on time series),
that'd look like this:

  normal_log(y[n,m] | mu[k] + alpha[k] * y[n, m-1], sigma[k])

> But I am not sure if that even makes sense. I guess my biggest problem is I find it difficult to formulate the likelihood function mathematically.

Yes, that's where you need to start with Stan.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
That’s very helpful. Thanks a lot.

Did you intentionally use alpha as the coefficient for the AR(1) component? In my code I use alpha as a prior on the mixture components. I figure it was just an arbitrary choice, but just to be sure… What kind of priors would be “normal” to use? The uniform seems improper, the goto for linear models is the half-cauchy but I’m not sure it applies in the case of mixture models (or does it?).

Anyway, I plugged it into the Stan model (https://gist.github.com/demodw/3641605a0962dc953fb5), but now I get an error when I try to run it using CmdStan with the Variational inference engine:

p(y | theta, mu, sigma, beta)_t = \sum_i^K theta_i * N(y_t | mu+beta[k]*y_{t-1}, sigma) for t = 2 .. T

These welcome messages mess up rstan 2.7.0-1. The easiest thing is probably to set the environmental variables R_PROFILE_USER and R_PROFILE_SITE to non-existent files before trying to install rstan from CRAN

Sys.setenv(R_PROFILE_USER = "foobar")
Sys.setenv(R_PROFILE_SITE = "foobar")

Then you can restart R and it should find your .Rprofile files again. If that doesn't work, then it is possible to install the development versions of everything. Or if you can wait a few days, new versions will be on CRAN.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jangho,

This one's easy. I'm not familiar with the distribution and I don't know the effect of having a discontinuity at mu == x, but this one's easy to code up:

functions {
  real subottin_log(real x, real alpha, real beta, real mu) {
     real y;
     y <- beta / (2 * alpha * exp(lgamma(1 / beta)) * exp(-pow(abs(x - mu) / alpha, beta)));
     return log(y);
  }
}

I didn't actually run it, so if there are typos, it might not compile. This isn't the most efficient code out there. Stan has the lgamma function, so I took the exp of the lgamma function, but if it'd be better if you worked directly in log space.

If you did that, inside the model block, you could do something like...

   x ~ subottin(alpha, beta, mu)

where any of those could be data or parameters.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users mailing list members

I am Daisuke from Japan. I start to learn statistical modeling and how to use Stan and RStan.
This is the first time to post message.

I have a question and a favor to ask of you.
1. I want to predict distribution of input by using distribution of output. Can I do it by using Stan?
2. If possible, would you explain very simple sample for this case.

I am a researcher on crashworthiness of structure. I hope that when distribution of output (deformation, …) is obtained, I want to predict distribution of characteristics of structure (stiffness, ultimate strength, …). In this case, relation between the input and output is non-linear and cannot be represented explicitly.

So, I suppose the following steps in order to predict

1) Mechanical simulations will be performed by using randomized characteristics following a probability density distribution.
2) The distribution of simulation results will be compared with that of experiment output.
3) The probability density distribution of characteristics will be updated by MCMC to minimize residual between the simulation result distribution and the experiment output distribution.

I think probability distribution in step 1 corresponds to prior probability and that in step 3 corresponds to posterior probability. So, I think I can apply Stan to this problem.

Can you advise on the situation? I have attached a PDF complementing my question. My question is “Case 2”.

Best Regards,
Daisuke

messages.body_plain:
You're sort of outlining all of Bayesian statistics, so it's
hard to know where to start in answering this question.

The steps (1)--(3) aren't quite right terminologically.  (1) is the
likelihood, not the prior.  (2) is what we call posterior predictive
checking.  (3) isn't quite right --- we fit posteriors given data,
likelihood and prior.

There's a chapter in the manual on Bayesian stats and one on using MCMC
for sampling that might be useful for you to understand if you want to
undertake computational Bayesian modeling.  It will also help to start
with some examples from your field or a related mechanical engineering
or safety trial application if they're relevant.

- Bob

messages.subject: convergence in Poisson with very large values
messages.subject_clean: convergence in Poisson with very large values
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

The attached model tries to fit a Poisson distribution to discrete counts that have an expectation of ca. 40,000,000.  I do know that the normal is going to be a very good approximation in these circumstances, but what if we wanted to stick with the Poisson.  Arguably, we should be able to fit it, shouldn't we?  And in fact, the glmer function in the lme4 R package seems to be able to do so.  But, rstan (v2.7) does a really poor job in this parameter space.  I suspect that this is because of the factorial in the Poisson likelihood and any associated overflow could be avoided by incrementing the log probability without the factorial, as it is a constant (but I haven't tried this yet).

The main question I had now was whether stan should be able to fit this model in the first place, especially as glmer seems able to return something sensible?  I've attached self-contained code that compares the two approaches.

Thanks
Andrew

>
> Thanks Ben.  I simplified this example quickly from something much more complicated so could have definitely been more efficient in terms of vectorizing by group (as Bob suggests) or using the Matt trick.

The Matt trick is not primarily about efficiency in the sense of how fast it takes to computer to execute a function; it is about changing the geometry of the posterior distribution so that Stan can sample from the posterior distribution efficiently (in the sense of quickly converging to the posterior distribution, having low dependence among consecutive draws, exploring the tails, etc.).

> So I guess I want to ask whether is there any good reason why we can't recover the estimates without the Matt trick, especially if it isn't an issue associated with the dropping the constants (which I had forgotten that Stan does).

In many cases with multilevel models, it is not possible for Stan to sample efficiently without the Matt trick. That isn't a universal rule but in this case, I think it is necessary.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
It might sample as written with reasonable initial values, or
with the centered parameterization (fully non Matt tricked version),

  group[k] ~ normal(intercept, sigma);

and then you don't need to add the intercept for mu.  You might also
get by with tighter priors.  But as written with our default inits you're
right it doesn't work.

The problem is that it's not converging in the warmup span given.  What
happens with the problem as originally written is that chains get stuck with
the wrong fixed effect with the group-level effects compensating with higher values
and hence a higher std deviation because values are (non-)centered around 0.

The centered parameterization can help here (opposite of the Matt trick),
as can tighter priors, which can tamp down the deviation of the group-level
effects.  It's difficult for the sampler to move away from this suboptimal solution
because of the correlation between the hierarchical standard deviation and the
values of the group effects.  You need to simultaneously move to lower
standard deviation and smaller group-level effects and higher fixed effect.
It's basically the usual problem in a hierarchical model as illustrated
by the funnel in the manual chapter on problematic posteriors.

It might also work as written with reasonable initial values.

- Bob

For (1), I think you would need a Jacobian correction. It may be the
most straightforward solution to code, but may not sample efficiently,
since diff will be < 0 for some parameters.

Whether (2) is appealing depends on what you are modeling. I would think
about making epsilon a parameter. Not sure about identification though,
do we know anything about x_{i,j} -- eg do they come from the same
distribution for a given j?

For (3) you might make

z_{i,j} = a_{i,j} x_{i,j} / y_i

and then z_i is in a 3-simplex. Then parametrize either in a_{i,j} or
x_{i,j}.

Unless there is a strong reason not to (again, depends on your model, of
which I don't have domain-specific knowledge), I would go for (2). I
have spent about a week recently coding up clever transformations for a
model with constraints similar to (1)/(3) (in spirit; they were actually
nonlinear), only to find that (2) makes more sense and is easier to
extend, and I could assign meaning to the error.

Best,

Tamas

Hi Bob

What makes you think that the chains are getting stuck and it is not something else?  I've tried jittering the stepsize and that doesn't seem to help.

The model that I am trying to fit has an observation-level random effect.  That is what you are seeing in the glmer code.  And this is often referred to as a Poisson-lognormal distribution.  Here is a widely-cited paper on it:  http://www.abdn.ac.uk/lambin-group/Papers/Paper%2041%202001%20Elston%20Tick%20aggregation%20Parasitology.pdf.  The observation-level effect essentially soaks up the residual error left over from the other terms and is useful for dealing with over-dispersion.

I have fitted this type of model many times in Stan without any issue.  It seems that this particular problem is confined to the large values of y.  If you divide y by 400,000 and round to integers, for example, the model fits fine in Stan (though remember to relax the informative prior on the intercept).  The estimates also match glmer.  Again, to me this flags up an issue with large integer values and Stan's Poisson calculations/sampling.

Thanks
Andrew

messages.body_plain:
I would not recommend 2, because I don't think you can easily fake
a hard constraint with a soft constraint.

The problem for (1) isn't so much that you need a Jacobian with this transform

>   x[i,1] <- (y[i] - a[i, 2] x[i, 2] - a[i, 3] x[i, 3]) / a[i, 1];

but rather that it's that you're trying to provide three distributions for
x[i,1:3] on what are effectively two variables, x[i,2:3] and a funciton of them.
So you need to work out what the implications are.  It's like you're doing
something like this:

  y[1] ~ foo(...);
  y[2] ~ foo(...);
  y[1] + y[2] ~ foo(...);

It's much easier to work with a model conceptually if you can imagine
the generative process leading to the data.

You can see an instance of that with the way we handle simplexes under the hood.
If you declare

  parameters {
    simplex[5] theta;
    ...

then there are really 4 underlying variables.  Under the hood Stan does
the transform and takes care of the Jacobian.  Then if you do this

  model {
    theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);

everything's OK because the Dirichlet has support over the simplexes.
But you're constraining things more and using mismatched distributions that aren't
distributions over your constrained variables.  It'd be like for the simplex doing this

  theta ~ normal(0, 1);

and then I'm not sure what it'd mean.  Someone else will hopefully know and
set us both straight here.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to both of you for the feedback.  Yes, I'm having a hard time thinking about how to handle the constraint.

Here's more about the generative process (good suggestion):

* I've got a set of blood samples.  Each sample is a mixture of K cell types (monocytes, lymphocytes, etc), and I've measured the fraction of each cell type in each sample.  I'm assuming for now that these measurements are noiseless.  The quantity a_{i, j} is the fraction of cell type j in sample i.

* I measure a substance of interest in each sample (my y_i terms).  I know that each cell type produces a different amount of the substance (x_{i, j} is the amount of substance produced by cell type j in sample i), and y_i = \sum_j a_{i, j} x_{i, j}.  There is variation in the amount of substance produced per cell type from sample to sample, and I know a priori that the distribution is log-normal.  Think of it as biological variation from person to person, and assume that the samples all come from different people.  More concretely, if I were able to get samples from a set of people that were purified so they contained only a single cell type, I know a priori that the amount of substance I'd measure in each sample would be distributed roughly log-normally.  (Each cell type j has its own log-normal parameters)

* There's measurement error in the mix as well, and I know a priori that the errors are multiplicative.

The model in which I've introduced the extra error term I think of as being a model in which I've got both biological and technical variation represented explicitly.  If I let the measurement error term be a parameter, I get identifiability problems, since increasing the technical variation is roughly equivalent to increasing all the sources of biological variation (i.e. the variances in the log-normals for individual cell types).

The constrained model is an attempt to assume the measurement error can be subsumed into the biological variation terms.

Adding in the extra multiplicative error term is an attempt to model the measurement error explicitly, and my making it a known quantity is a way to get around identifiability issues.

Does that make more sense?

Geoff

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am doing a fairly straightforward nonlinear curve-fitting problem with independent Gaussian errors. I have set it up in pystan and am pretty happy with the results. (For the aficionados, I am fitting sub-millimetre galaxy spectral energy distributions.)

One nice way to visualise the results is to actually show the "best-fit" curve (or, better, various samples from the posterior), but at many more x values (in my case, observed wavelengths) than the small number where I have actual data.

However, in order to do that, I basically need to recode the model in python and use matplotlib to make the curve using the parameters that I get from the get_posterior_mean() method (and/or from a subset of the posterior samples if I'm doing more serious model checking).

I could probably do some of this within Stan using "generated quantities" but this would require a large number of these (for each of the x values) which would be inefficient and difficult to play with interactively.

A simple solution to this problem would be to write the fitting function in the actual function block (although this isn't currently how I have the code structured) and expose this to python. As of now, definitions in the function block is only available within Stan, but I imagine it should be possible to make them available (as the various log_probabilty functions are). Any chance of this happening?

Yours,

Andrew

> Bob, your comment spurred an interesting thought:
>
> One way to think about the constrained joint distribution of the x[i, j] for sample i is that it's the unconstrained distribution restricted to the hyperplane on which the constraint is satisfied, i.e. where x[i,1] = (y[i] - a[i, 2] x[i, 2] - a[i, 3] x[i, 3]) / a[i, 1].  The headache is that what I want is a conditional probability where the condition is the hyperplane constraint, i.e. I need to normalize the constrained joint distribution, and the normalization factor depends on the parameters of interest.  If I'm understanding correctly, I need to compute the normalization each step of the sampling process along the lines of what's described in section 13.10 of BDA3 (pp 345-6).  (The soft constraint is similar but involves integrating a different function.)
>
> Does this make sense?
>
> On Tuesday, September 15, 2015 at 3:20:48 PM UTC-7, Geoff Davis wrote:
> Thanks to both of you for the feedback.  Yes, I'm having a hard time thinking about how to handle the constraint.
>
> Here's more about the generative process (good suggestion):
>
> * I've got a set of blood samples.  Each sample is a mixture of K cell types (monocytes, lymphocytes, etc), and I've measured the fraction of each cell type in each sample.  I'm assuming for now that these measurements are noiseless.  The quantity a_{i, j} is the fraction of cell type j in sample i.
>
> * I measure a substance of interest in each sample (my y_i terms).  I know that each cell type produces a different amount of the substance (x_{i, j} is the amount of substance produced by cell type j in sample i), and y_i = \sum_j a_{i, j} x_{i, j}.  There is variation in the amount of substance produced per cell type from sample to sample, and I know a priori that the distribution is log-normal.  Think of it as biological variation from person to person, and assume that the samples all come from different people.  More concretely, if I were able to get samples from a set of people that were purified so they contained only a single cell type, I know a priori that the amount of substance I'd measure in each sample would be distributed roughly log-normally.  (Each cell type j has its own log-normal parameters)
>
> * There's measurement error in the mix as well, and I know a priori that the errors are multiplicative.
>
> The model in which I've introduced the extra error term I think of as being a model in which I've got both biological and technical variation represented explicitly.  If I let the measurement error term be a parameter, I get identifiability problems, since increasing the technical variation is roughly equivalent to increasing all the sources of biological variation (i.e. the variances in the log-normals for individual cell types).
>
> The constrained model is an attempt to assume the measurement error can be subsumed into the biological variation terms.
>
> Adding in the extra multiplicative error term is an attempt to model the measurement error explicitly, and my making it a known quantity is a way to get around identifiability issues.
>
> Does that make more sense?
>
> Geoff

messages.subject: non-convergence with Poisson with lambda approx exp(17) approx 25M
messages.subject_clean: non-convergence with Poisson with lambda approx exp(17) approx 25M
messages.body_plain:
This definitely won't converge.  I'm attaching a standalone Stan model
and R dump formatted data so Michael might be able to take a look at it.
The basic idea is that there's an item-level lognormal random effect
contributing to the mean parameter for the Poisson --- it's an alternative
to the gamma you find in the negative binomial for overdispersion that
makes the whole thing compatible with being run as a GLM.

The basic behavior really jumps around with the epochs of fast/slow
adaptation, so I think they may be overtuning in some sense.  It then
always drifts during sampling --- that is, even 20K warmup iterations starting
from small initial step size (0.001) and high acceptance target (0.99) doesn't
get to where it should.

I'm not sure what's going on.  But it's definitely not converging.  I
tried much tighter priors, not using intervals on sd, +/- Matt trick, etc.
I tried very small step sizes, very large tree depth, etc.  Some just
ground to a halt so I didn't have patience to go on.

I wonder if it could be something as basic as scale required for regularization
in our mass matrix estimation.

lme4 recovers the parameters no problem (and almost instantly, to boot).

What appears to happen is that each chain gets stuck in its own local
part of the parameter space --- that is, it only seems to be weakly
identified.

With much smaller sizes, the OP (atzap) said it converges.  I haven't
tried.

Of course, in this case, a normal approximation is probably warranted, so
I'm not too worried about this particular model --- it's just that I want
to understand what's going on with the sampler.

- Bob

On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 4:10:26 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> validate transformed params: Gmeasured[k0__][13] is -0.000140616, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

This means that the expression that generates the elements of Gmeasured is not positive by construction. In the usual case where the amount of posterior mass on the Gmeasured margins to the left of zero is not a constant, then your priors on the things in the parameters block would not integrate to a constant over the declared parameter space. If the amount of truncated mass is, in fact, a constant, then the posterior kernel is valid, but the sampling from that posterior distribution is very inefficient in Stan.

Either way, this is a problem, which is why we are not making it easy to avoid looking at the Informational Messages. But you can call stan() or sampling() with open_progress = TRUE to look at them in a web browser rather than the console.

Ben

So I moved Gmeasured to the transformed parameters section and set the constraint between 0 and 1 there. Before I upgraded, I did not receive a single one of these messages.

If it is in the model block, it does not (and cannot) check whether the quantity is negative, so you wouldn't get an Informational Message. But if the quantity must be positive and is not, then you have the same substantive problem whether it is defined in the transformed parameters block or the model block. The problem that the Informational Messages are annoying is minor relative to the problem of not drawing from the intended posterior or not doing so with sufficient efficiency.

> On Sep 17, 2015, at 5:50 PM, Daniel Berman <daniel....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This problem began when I upgraded rstan recently. It said that I could no longer constrain a variable within the model block. So I moved Gmeasured to the transformed parameters section and set the constraint between 0 and 1 there. Before I upgraded, I did not receive a single one of these messages.
>
> On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 5:12:48 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, September 17, 2015 at 4:10:26 PM UTC-4, Daniel Berman wrote:
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
> validate transformed params: Gmeasured[k0__][13] is -0.000140616, but must be greater than or equal to 0
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.
>
> This means that the expression that generates the elements of Gmeasured is not positive by construction. In the usual case where the amount of posterior mass on the Gmeasured margins to the left of zero is not a constant, then your priors on the things in the parameters block would not integrate to a constant over the declared parameter space. If the amount of truncated mass is, in fact, a constant, then the posterior kernel is valid, but the sampling from that posterior distribution is very inefficient in Stan.
>
> Either way, this is a problem, which is why we are not making it easy to avoid looking at the Informational Messages. But you can call stan() or sampling() with open_progress = TRUE to look at them in a web browser rather than the console.
>
> Ben

> The problem arises from the fact that there are a large number of unconstrained matrix parameters multiplied together so I'm assuming that the problem arises from the complexity of what is going on.

> I doubt it, but it is hard to say without knowing what the informational message is.

messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to add a geostatistical component to a hierarchical regression with random intercepts.

y[i] ~ N(alpha[site[i]] + X[i]*beta, sigma)
alpha ~ MVN(mu, Sigma), Sigma = exp(-lambda * D)

Where alpha is a k dimensional vector, mu is a k-vector of 0's, D is a k by k distance matrix, and lambda is a positive parameter modelling the strength of the spatial autocorrelation.

The model keeps running into max treedepth errors; increasing the parameter up to 12 gives no improved response, and I'm still waiting for the runs with larger values to finish.  The model is also occasionally sampling lambda as 0, resulting in a Sigma of all 1's, causing a rejected Metropolis step; I'm unsure what prior would work best to avoid this.

I've tried using the multivariate Matt trick, but I'm not convinced I'm using it correctly.  I'm not particularly familiar with Cholesky decomposition, so I am wondering if I misspecified the model.

Any assistance would be greatly appreciated

You can certainly use a matrix or 2d-array as the return type, but you can't return a pair of differently named variables.

More generally, for ragged data structures to return, You can roll up the vectors, and unroll them later, which is the approach I am using. It's inelegant, but avoids the limitation you are discussing.

messages.subject: parameterization of additive ICAR model
messages.subject_clean: parameterization of additive ICAR model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am seeking advice about parameterization of ICAR GMRF model. I’m trying to fit a model to incidence by time and age: g(t,a) = f(t) + f(a) + f(t,a), where each of the functions have ICAR(1) priors in one dimension for f(t) and f(a) and two dimensions for f(t,a). The model formulation reflects the expectation that there is a dominant age and time trend, with smaller deviations in the f(a,t) term (in which we are quite interested).

The model fits well when I fit only the additive terms f(t) + f(a), or when I fit only the bivariate function f(t,a), but when I fit the additive model g(t,a) = f(t) + f(a) + f(t,a) the step size becomes very very small, it reaches maximum tree depth, and n_divergent is high. I suspect that the problem may be related to the variance parameter associated with f(t,a) is much smaller than the variance on f(t) and f(a).

The likelihood for the real data is more complicated and computationally expensive, but for the purposes of exploring the model structure I’ve created a simple Poisson likelihood (attached). I’ve parameterized the model in two ways (1) parameterizing the values of the response g(t,a) and applying linear transformations to recover the underlying f(t), f(a), f(t,a), and (2) directly parameterizing f(t), f(a), and f(t,a) [with sum-to-zero constraints for identifiability].

When I simulate random data without any trends (such that the variance for the three additive terms are of similar magnitude), the model converges well and fast. But when I simulate more realistic data, such that the variation in f(t,a) is much less than in f(t) and f(a) dimensions, I get much the same as with the real data -- very small step size, and poor convergence. I’m wondering if anyone has advice for better parameterization of the model? (Or if I’ve done something obviously silly...)

In other threads about GMRFs, I’ve seen suggestions to consider applying the ‘Matt trick’, but wasn’t sure how to apply it to the improper covariance matrix for 2D ICAR(1) prior for f(t,a).

Thanks,
Jeff

messages.subject: rstan 2.8.0 seems to be out. And fucks me sideways... How can I solve ?
messages.subject_clean: rstan 2.8.0 seems to be out. And fucks me sideways... How can I solve ?
messages.body_plain:
A routine update of my CRAN packages got me rstan 2.8.0 (and StanHeaders 2.8.0), which is (yet) unannunced. And I'm fucked...

I used to dump the traceplots of my MCMC run on a multipage PDF with something along the lines of :

    PN <- F1@model_pars
    SLPN <- c("mu", "sigma", "rho", "delta")
    pdf(file="Check1-1.pdf", pointsize=12, width=7, height=10,
    paper="special", title="Charpentier - MCMC trace checking : study-level parameters")
    traceplot(F1, pars=SLPN, inc_warmup=FALSE, nrow=5, ncol=3)
    dev.off()

Those four parameters being (not so small) vectors (78 parameters total), I used to get a dense multipage PDF.

This worked up to rstan 2.7.0. rstan now uses ggplot2 to create a traceplot, which can be customized to death thanks to ggplot2 options. Nice (and commendable) idea...

Do you see a quick way to get rstan::traceplot to do that ?

By the way, the "ask=TRUE" option of the interactive version (probably inherited from coda's "traceplot") was a nice idea for interactive work. Could we get back something like that ?

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

You've probably found this already, but all the fonts, axis tick marks, titles, etc. can be customized by adding theme elements (there are many examples if you look at help("theme", package = "ggplot2")). It's a bit strange at first if you're used to the base plotting functions in R, but once you get used to it there are a lot of advantages (of course there are some cases when ggplot makes things hard.) As for package management for reproducibility, I second Mike Lawrence's suggestion of packrat. It's integrated with RStudio too, which makes it easier to use.

On Thursday, December 18, 2014 at 5:55:24 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If R-hat is NaN and n_eff is not NaN, it's almost certainly
> a precision problemin the arithmetic.
>
> Could you send us a model and data set for which it happens so
> we can diagnose?
>
> There may be loss of arithmetic precision in R-hat compared to
> what we could do ideally.  The problem is that floating point
> subtraction of values close to each other results in so-called
> catastrophic cancellation, losing an arbitrary amount of precision.
> Something like Welford's algorithm is required to maintain stability
> for sample variance calculations, and I'm not sure how PyStan has implemented
> R-hat.
>
> For example, this model is problematic arithmetically:
>
> fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(1,1e-20); }")
>
> and produces
>
>           mean  se_mean       sd      2.5%       25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff         Rhat
> y            1      0.0        0         1         1   1   1     1  4000          Inf
> lp__ -15407440 422002.9 26689805 -61629758 -15407440   0   0     0  4000 1.500106e+14
>
>
> There's really nothing we can do about such models numerically.  What
> you have to do from a user perspective is use a parameterizations
>
>   z = y - 1,
>
> which can be handled stably because you can represent numbers close to zero well.
>
> parameters { real z; } model { z ~ normal(0,1e-20); }
>
> The problem is that there's still no way to represent y = z + 1, but
> you can get close to log(y) by using
>
>   log_y <- log1p(z);
>
> We're gradually pulling all these implementations back into
> the core Stan C++ code, so at least we'll only have one fix to make
> for issues like this in the near future.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  I'm going to drop the above discussion into a new section on
>       arithmetic in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
>       or maybe an entire chapter on arithmetic stability of various operators.
>

> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.body_plain:
(Sorry if this is a dupe --- it was sitting unsent in my outbox.)

That makes it much clearer what's going on in terms of parameters
and the generative process.

So I think your (1) is on the right track:

> 1) Express x[i, 1] in terms of x[i, 2] and x[i, 3], e.g.
>
> real diff;
> for (i in 1:nsample) {
>   x[i, 2] ~ lognormal(mu_2, sigma_2);
>   x[i, 3] ~ lognormal(mu_3, sigma_3);
>   diff <- (y[i] - a[i, 2] x[i, 2] - a[i, 3] x[i, 3]) / a[i, 1];
>   diff ~ lognormal(mu_1, sigma_1);
> }

The main issue you're going to have with this given that
y and a are known but x is not, is that you have an implicit
constraint

  y[i] > a[i,2] * x[i,2] + a[i,3] * x[i,3]

that follows from (diff > 0) and (a > 0).

Because Stan doesn't let you custom constrain each member of a
matrix like x, the only recourse I can see is to write your own
custom transforms and apply the appropriate Jacobians.

That is, constrain

  0 <  x[i,2]  <  y[i] / a[i,2]

  0  < x[i,3]  <  (y[i] - a[i,2] * x[i,2]) / a[i,3]

That means declaring x_raw unconstrained, then inverse logit
and scale transforming it and applying the Jacobians.

Then you're in a position to use the diff formulation.  But it's
a lot of work.  Maybe someone else will see a clever way to encode
this.

- Bob

> On Sep 15, 2015, at 6:20 PM, Geoff Davis <ge...@geoffdavis.net> wrote:
>
> Thanks to both of you for the feedback.  Yes, I'm having a hard time thinking about how to handle the constraint.
>
> Here's more about the generative process (good suggestion):
>
> * I've got a set of blood samples.  Each sample is a mixture of K cell types (monocytes, lymphocytes, etc), and I've measured the fraction of each cell type in each sample.  I'm assuming for now that these measurements are noiseless.  The quantity a_{i, j} is the fraction of cell type j in sample i.
>
> * I measure a substance of interest in each sample (my y_i terms).  I know that each cell type produces a different amount of the substance (x_{i, j} is the amount of substance produced by cell type j in sample i), and y_i = \sum_j a_{i, j} x_{i, j}.  There is variation in the amount of substance produced per cell type from sample to sample, and I know a priori that the distribution is log-normal.  Think of it as biological variation from person to person, and assume that the samples all come from different people.  More concretely, if I were able to get samples from a set of people that were purified so they contained only a single cell type, I know a priori that the amount of substance I'd measure in each sample would be distributed roughly log-normally.  (Each cell type j has its own log-normal parameters)
>
> * There's measurement error in the mix as well, and I know a priori that the errors are multiplicative.
>
> The model in which I've introduced the extra error term I think of as being a model in which I've got both biological and technical variation represented explicitly.  If I let the measurement error term be a parameter, I get identifiability problems, since increasing the technical variation is roughly equivalent to increasing all the sources of biological variation (i.e. the variances in the log-normals for individual cell types).
>
> The constrained model is an attempt to assume the measurement error can be subsumed into the biological variation terms.
>
> Adding in the extra multiplicative error term is an attempt to model the measurement error explicitly, and my making it a known quantity is a way to get around identifiability issues.
>
> Does that make more sense?
>
> Geoff
>
>
> On Tuesday, September 15, 2015 at 2:39:29 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I would not recommend 2, because I don't think you can easily fake
> a hard constraint with a soft constraint.
>
> The problem for (1) isn't so much that you need a Jacobian with this transform
>
> >   x[i,1] <- (y[i] - a[i, 2] x[i, 2] - a[i, 3] x[i, 3]) / a[i, 1];
>
> but rather that it's that you're trying to provide three distributions for
> x[i,1:3] on what are effectively two variables, x[i,2:3] and a funciton of them.
> So you need to work out what the implications are.  It's like you're doing
> something like this:
>
>   y[1] ~ foo(...);
>   y[2] ~ foo(...);
>   y[1] + y[2] ~ foo(...);
>
> It's much easier to work with a model conceptually if you can imagine
> the generative process leading to the data.
>
> You can see an instance of that with the way we handle simplexes under the hood.
> If you declare
>
>   parameters {
>     simplex[5] theta;
>     ...
>
> then there are really 4 underlying variables.  Under the hood Stan does
> the transform and takes care of the Jacobian.  Then if you do this
>
>   model {
>     theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
>
> everything's OK because the Dirichlet has support over the simplexes.
> But you're constraining things more and using mismatched distributions that aren't
> distributions over your constrained variables.  It'd be like for the simplex doing this
>
>   theta ~ normal(0, 1);
>
> and then I'm not sure what it'd mean.  Someone else will hopefully know and
> set us both straight here.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Sep 14, 2015, at 8:34 PM, Geoff Davis <ge...@geoffdavis.net> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Stan folks -
> >
> > I've got a measurement that I'm trying to model as a convex combination of k log-normals.  The weights in the convex combination are known and vary from measure to measure; what I'm trying to do is to estimate the parameters of the log-normals.
> >
> > I've used Stan happily for HLMs where everything is Gaussian, but I'm a bit puzzled about how to express this new kind of relationship since the log-normals don't conveniently collapse.
> >
> > For concreteness, suppose
> >
> > y_i = a_{i,1} x_{i,1} + a_{i, 2} x_{i, 2} + a_{i, 3} x_{i, 3}
> >
> > where
> >
> > x_{i, j} ~ lognormal(mu_j, sigma_j)
> >
> > and I have priors on mu_j and sigma_j.
> >
> > The values of y_i are all observed.
> > The values a_{i, j} are all known, and for all i, a_{i, 1} + a_{i, 2} + a_{i, 3} = 1.
> >
> >
> > A few possibilities:
> >
> > 1) Express x[i, 1] in terms of x[i, 2] and x[i, 3], e.g.
> >
> > real diff;
> > for (i in 1:nsample) {
> >   x[i, 2] ~ lognormal(mu_2, sigma_2);
> >   x[i, 3] ~ lognormal(mu_3, sigma_3);
> >   diff <- (y[i] - a[i, 2] x[i, 2] - a[i, 3] x[i, 3]) / a[i, 1];
> >   diff ~ lognormal(mu_1, sigma_1);
> > }
> >
> > 2) Introduce a small source of additional noise with known variance.  Then I can declare something like
> >
> > for (i in 1:nsample) {
> >   x[i, 1] ~ lognormal(mu_1, sigma_1);
> >   x[i, 2] ~ lognormal(mu_2, sigma_2);
> >   x[i, 3] ~ lognormal(mu_3, sigma_3);
> >   y[i] ~ lognormal(log(a[i, 1] * x[i, 1] + a[i, 2] * x[i, 2] + a[i, 3] * x[i, 3]), epsilon);
> > }
> >
> > 3) Something else?  I'm wondering if there's some sort of trick I need to do along the lines of the way Stan deals with simplexes.
> >
> > Thanks!
> >
> > Geoff
> >

sounds like that's not what's happening here. If you can reproduce the
problem with model code and data you're willing to share, I can look
into it.  If that's not possible, I'd suggest trying to run the model in
RStan and seeing if rhat is displayed.

Best,

Allen

messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the delayed response! That informational message in ADVI comes up when it has a numerically unstable sample. The default should allow it to drop the point and continue resampling, so don’t worry too much about the informational message. It generally means that either the current initialization is bad (i.e. the informational message happens all the time in the beginning of the procedure), or the model is simply hard to fit.

If the initialization is bad, and there’s no way to fix it on the user end, then I suggest you up the number of grad_samples to make the gradient updates more reliable. Hope this helps.

Dustin

The data I used can be found at https://gist.github.com/demodw/1df3f5141819daea69e2 in R format. I suspect the initialisation values might be too much off, but I am not sure how to come up with a better guesstimate than Stan. messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Sampler rejects multinomial logit with random intercepts
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone for your patient advice. I have tried to implement your suggestions but I'm not quite there--still getting rejected for a mismatch in the likelihood statement. Here is the Stan code:

>
> > data {
> >   int<lower=2> C;           # categories of y
> >   int<lower=0> N;           # observations
> >   int<lower=1> K;           # variables
> >   int<lower=1> J;           # number of counties
> >   int<lower=1> id[N];       # county id

> >   int<lower=1,upper=C> y[N];    # categorical outcomes

> >   vector[K] xmat[N];        # predictors
> > }
> >
> > parameters {
> >   vector[J] b0_free[C-1];      # county intercepts

> >   vector[C-1] B0_free;        # level 2 intercepts

> >   matrix[C-1,K] beta_free;    # effects coefficients

> >   vector<lower=0>[C-1] sigma_b0_free;  # intercept variances
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> >   vector[J] b0[C];            # county intercepts
> >   vector[C] B0;               # intercept hyperparameters
> >   matrix[C,K] beta;           # effects coefficients

> >   vector[C] sigma_b0;
> >   for (k in 1:K)

> >     beta[1,k] <- 0;

> >   for (c in 2:C)

> >     for (k in 1:K)
> >       beta[c,k] <- beta_free[c-1,k];

> >   for (j in 1:J) {
> >     b0[1,j] <- 0;
> >       for (c in 2:C) {

> >         b0[c,j] <- b0_free[c-1,j];
> >   }}

> >   B0[1] <- 0;
> >   for (c in 1:C-1)
> >     B0[c+1] <- B0_free[c];
> >
> >   sigma_b0[1] <- 0;

> >   for (c in 2:C)

> >     sigma_b0[c] <- sigma_b0_free[c-1];
> > }
> > model {

> >   to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0,5);
> >   for (c in 1:C-1)
> >       b0_free[c] ~ normal(B0_free[c], sigma_b0_free[c]) ;

> >   sigma_b0_free ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
> >   # likelihood
> >   for (n in 1:N)

> >     y[n] ~ categorical_logit(b0[id[n]] + beta * xmat[n]);
> > }
>
And here is the error message:

> > Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:

> > Exception thrown at line 56:
> > add: Rows of m1 (12) and rows of m2 (4) must match in size
> > If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable terror occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

So the program is treating b0 like a JxC matrix (probably a weird way to say it), so it can't be added to beta, which is CxK. I tried redefining b0 as an array of J C-vectors (vector[C] b0[J], and b0_free accordingly). The model ran but produced wrong results. So I'm stuck, and would very much appreciate your advice.

John

>

On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 9:47:47 PM UTC-8, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, January 22, 2015 at 10:26:18 PM UTC-5, John Sutton wrote:
> > Jeez you're quick--thanks! I took you to mean that the declaration of b0 should be changed to
> >
> > > vector[J] b0[C];
> > >
> > though I confess I don't know what that statement really means.
>
> This is Stan / C++ is very similar to the R construct of a list of length C where each list element is a numeric vector of length J. So, you could access that in R with
>
> b0[[c]][j]
>
> to obtain the j-th element of the c-th vector. In Stan, it is just
>
> b0[c,j]
>
> or
>
> b0[c][j]
>
> > Anyway, now it's rejected for a different--but perhaps related--reason, with a series of messages like:
>
> Declare the standard deviations with a positivity constraint
>
> vector<lower=0>[C-1] sigma_b0_free
>
> Then, you would be two steps closer to having it work.
>
> Ben

messages.body_plain:
It's actually not so easy to make it work out that way, although it would be nice.

rstan takes longer to get through the CRAN process than StanHeaders, but it can't go up in advance of StanHeaders because it requires StanHeaders. The CRAN process is also pretty standardized in that once StanHeaders makes it through, it's through, although the time until all binaries are built can vary. So StanHeaders would end up being available first even if the two were submitted at exactly the same time.
