On Mon, Sep 21, 2015 at 10:26 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
> Dear Paula,
>
> PyStan's rhat calculation has some bugs associated with it. In the
> future, PyStan will use the same rhat code as CmdStan uses.
>
> There are known issues when the variance of the parameter is zero but it
> sounds like that's not what's happening here. If you can reproduce the
> problem with model code and data you're willing to share, I can look
> into it.  If that's not possible, I'd suggest trying to run the model in
> RStan and seeing if rhat is displayed.
>
> Best,
>
> Allen
>
>
> On 09/21, Paula Sarkis wrote:
> > I have around 100 parameters. All the parameters have n_eff = 6668 and Rhat
> > = 1.0 except for only 1 parameter (the most important one). This parameter
> > has n_eff = 6668 but Rhat = nan
> >
> > I am running MCMC with 10,000 iterations, warmup = 5,000 and with 4 chains.
> > So that's a total of 20,000 draws. n_eff of lp is 3938 and Rhat = 1.0.
> >
> > Any idea why I am getting Rhat  = nan?
> >
> > On Mon, Sep 21, 2015 at 7:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > > The manual provides the formula in the MCMC chapter.
> > >
> > > I don't know that there's a way for R-hat to be NaN without
> > > n_eff being NaN.
> > >
> > > If PyStan lets you dump the output in the CSV format which
> > > CmdStan can read, you could check that way.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > > On Sep 21, 2015, at 12:00 PM, Paula Sarkis <paula.s...@gmail.com>
> > > wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Hello,
> > > >
> > > > I am having the same problem. The trace plot looks perfect however the
> > > value of Rhat is nan.
> > > >
> > > > Can you please give me some details on how to evaluate n_eff for each
> > > parameter. Also, how to evaluate lp. I've been having the 'nan' problem
> > > with rhat many times now, I want to double check whether my model is ill
> > > defined or if the problem is from python.
> > > >
> > > > Cheers,
> > > > Paula
> > > >
> > > > On Thursday, December 18, 2014 at 5:55:24 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > If R-hat is NaN and n_eff is not NaN, it's almost certainly
> > > > a precision problemin the arithmetic.
> > > >
> > > > Could you send us a model and data set for which it happens so
> > > > we can diagnose?
> > > >
> > > > There may be loss of arithmetic precision in R-hat compared to
> > > > what we could do ideally.  The problem is that floating point
> > > > subtraction of values close to each other results in so-called
> > > > catastrophic cancellation, losing an arbitrary amount of precision.
> > > > Something like Welford's algorithm is required to maintain stability
> > > > for sample variance calculations, and I'm not sure how PyStan has
> > > implemented
> > > > R-hat.
> > > >
> > > > For example, this model is problematic arithmetically:
> > > >
> > > > fit <- stan(model_code = "parameters { real y; } model { y ~
> > > normal(1,1e-20); }")
> > > >
> > > > and produces
> > > >
> > > >           mean  se_mean       sd      2.5%       25% 50% 75% 97.5%
> > > n_eff         Rhat
> > > > y            1      0.0        0         1         1   1   1     1
> > > 4000          Inf
> > > > lp__ -15407440 422002.9 26689805 -61629758 -15407440   0   0     0  4000
> > > 1.500106e+14
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > There's really nothing we can do about such models numerically.  What
> > > > you have to do from a user perspective is use a parameterizations
> > > >
> > > >   z = y - 1,
> > > >
> > > > which can be handled stably because you can represent numbers close to
> > > zero well.
> > > >
> > > > parameters { real z; } model { z ~ normal(0,1e-20); }
> > > >
> > > > The problem is that there's still no way to represent y = z + 1, but
> > > > you can get close to log(y) by using
> > > >
> > > >   log_y <- log1p(z);
> > > >
> > > > We're gradually pulling all these implementations back into
> > > > the core Stan C++ code, so at least we'll only have one fix to make
> > > > for issues like this in the near future.
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > > P.S.  I'm going to drop the above discussion into a new section on
> > > >       arithmetic in the problematic posteriors chapter of the manual
> > > >       or maybe an entire chapter on arithmetic stability of various
> > > operators.
> > > >
> > > > > On Dec 18, 2014, at 11:40 AM, Jesse Bloom <jesse...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > I sometimes get Rhat values of "nan" when using PyStan. This happens
> > > for certain data sets repeatedly. I think I get these values for variables
> > > that are actually very close to zero and seem well converged based on the
> > > effective sample size (n_eff) values. Is this a bug in stan?

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, September 14, 2015 at 4:44:58 AM UTC-7, Daisuke Ito wrote:
> Hello, Bob
> Thank you very much for your courteous reply.
>
> I understand I should learn Bayesian statistics much more.
> I try to check  the manual on Bayesian stats and one on using MCMC
> for sampling.
>
> Daisuke
>

I suggest starting with simple example problems to learn basic concepts. For example, a variety of spherical balls whose weight and diameter you know fall a certain distance through a fluid in a certain time (your data is weight, diameter, height, time) infer the viscosity of the fluid. You will need to know something about drag coefficients at different reynolds numbers for a sphere, and solve an ODE.

http://www.chem.mtu.edu/~fmorriso/DataCorrelationForSphereDrag2013.pdf

Once you understand how to do that problem, you will understand much more about your real problem.

To do this problem you could: choose a viscosity. Using an ODE solver and the drag coefficient curve given in above pdf, simulate the fall of several balls of different sizes, to calculate the fall time. Add a little bit of noise to your fall time to simulate measurement error. Create a data table (alternatively, if you have access to a variety of balls and a tank of water or oil, you could do the actual experiment!)

Now, define a Stan model to do the inference:

Define your data vectors: weight, diameter, height, fall time
Define your parameter: viscosity.
Define a prior over viscosity expressing the approximate range for viscosity.

Define the simulation using Stan's ODE solver, see Stan manual.
Define the likelihood function using output of ODE (predicted fall times) together with the data, and the measurement error model.

Run the Stan model to get posterior distribution for viscosity parameter.

> On Sep 22, 2015, at 2:43 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The Stan estimates should be ML estimates, not penalized.  The penalized likelihood option is not available yet.

Yes it is!  Check out the maximum likelihood chapter of the manual
for examples on how to write models for maximum likelihood and how
to add penalty terms (e.g., L1, L2, elastic net or user-defined).

You'll get penalized maximum likelihood if you add a penalty term.
For instance, in a linear regression, the vectorized form of the
likelihood is this:

   y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma);

If you just use that in the model, you get maximum likelihood.

If you want a penalty function on beta, say unit L2 normalized with
shrinkage to zero, you'd add this to the model

  increment_log_prob(-0.5 * beta' * beta);

or equivalently,

  beta ~ normal(0, 1);

You can similarly penalize sigma, though that's less common in
my limited experience with penalized MLE.

>  If you want a better answer about why your estimates are different you might want to present your estimates here (preferably from a couple of starting values for each algorithm), the likeliest answer is that the differences are numerical and not practically significant.  For starters the MATLAB and Stan code might use different tolerances.

Exactly --- the differences should be within the tolerances of both
algorithms.

- Bob

Thanks for input everyone!

I have three i7 machines (servers) and my desktop pc (also i7). The servers don't have X11 nor in fact any DE installed. Even if they had, it is inconvenient for me to setup stan simulation each time with remote desktop. I would run two 6 chain simulations in parallel per machine. Say I want to do 8 simulations. The simulations don't take long, but it does make difference whether they run 12 minutes (single machine) or 3 minutes (all 4 machines). Furthermore the machines have only single 128GB ssd drive (half of it set up as memory swap) and I can't afford to keep my whole data stack on each server with rsync.

So I'm looking for a solution that handles all my (say 8) simulations across all 4 machines including the data transfer with a single command. I'm going to investigate ipython some more. I'm afraid ipython uses pickle dumps to transfer the data and I'm not sure how well pystan supports pickling.

Ideally, I would love to have a stan controller that is fed a set of models, datasets and instructions about how to match the two and how many chains to run in each case. One would also provide info about the servers - how many machines and how many jobs/chains can be run in parrallel on each. Then  the controller goes to the servers and distributes all chains such that each machine is under full load until all jobs are assigned.

Daniel are your scripts available online? Would you mind to share them? I hope they don't use some esoteric cluster scripting language.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling for count regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] scaling for count regression
messages.body_plain:
Not necessarily.  There are two factors at work here — the mean
response and the variance of the data.  In most continuous settings
we can rescale the data which corresponds to shifting and scaling
the parameters.  In the discrete case we cannot rescale at all —
an integer divided by a real is not longer an integer, same for
addition/subtraction — and such a transformation wouldn’t have
the same corresponding effect on parameters anyways.  At least
not exactly.

You can write the function in Stan. If there's an iterative algorithm, that doesn't necessarily pose a problem. The autodiff will work through the iterative algorithm. (One of the benefits of autodiff compared to symbolic differentiation.)

There might be some speed gains if you implemented it in c++ directly, especially if you have the gradients with respect to all the parameters of the model, but if it were me, I'd start with a full Stan implementation.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] programming user-defined functions (C++, or another language)
messages.body_plain:
This is exactly what Michael was warning against --- naively
autodiffing an iterative algorithm.  And both Michael and Daniel
are right.  It can work to just autodiff an iterative algorithm,
but it can have bad numerical properties.  So it's better in terms of
both efficiency and numerical stability to write a separate iterative
algorithm for the derivative that takes its numerical properties
into account.

I also want to qualify that for a full Stan implementation of
a function, you need not only first-order derivatives, but also
second- and third-order.  Those usually come about through a templated
implementation of fvar<T> where T is either a var or fvar<var>.
But the same logic applies there --- autodiffing the first-order
Jacobian code to get the Hessian may not be stable.   But if all you
need to do is HMC, you can get by with just the var implementation,
which only needs the Jacobian.

Yes, the Stan Math Library is full of examples in C++.

I'm guessing the Julia to Stan combo shot will require you to know
more about C++, not less, than implementing it in C++ directly.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] scaling for count regression
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] scaling for count regression
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can do that, but I found it didn't make much difference.
We had a discussion here recently of a Poisson with parameters
on the scale of exp(alpha), where alpha is on the order of exp(17 + epsilon).
Unfortunately, taking the parameter to be (17 + epsilon) instead of alpha
didn't help.  So it's still an open problem for us.

I'm guessing the problem lies in the derivatives, which are going
to be super-sensitive out in this region due to the exp() scaling.

Of course, in the simple Poisson case, you can just move to a normal
approximation when counts are on the order of 1 billion.

- Bob

On Wednesday, September 23, 2015 at 7:07:19 AM UTC-7, Daisuke Ito wrote:
>
> Hello, Daniel
> Thank you very much for your courteous reply.
>
> What you suggested looks good example.
>
> I have one question.
> Is the ODE I should solve the following?
> If it is correct, I try to do this simulation.
>
> Sincerely yours,
> Daisuke Ito
>
> --------------------------------------------------
> mv'=-mg+{6πRηv+C 10.5×Cd×ρπ(R^2)×(v^2)}
> where
> v: velocity in falling direction.
> v'=dv/dt
> η: viscosity
> R: radius of ball
> ρ: density
>

I think you want

mv' = -mg + rho*4/3*pi*R^3 + Cd * rho * pi * R^2 v^2 / 2  + O(R * mu * v)

where rho is fluid density, R is ball radius, v is velocity, mu is dynamic viscosity. I'm not sure if your constant is correct for the linear in v term but it could well be.

On the right the first term is from gravity, the second from bouyancy, the third from piston drag, and the fourth from skin friction

You can divide the whole thing by mg and get into dimensionless form which might help you decide whether you can ignore skin friction for example.

I couldn't find what you were referring to in Chapter 6 of Gelman
and Hill.  Are you talking about where you mention exposure being
a multiplicative factor?

The formula for the mean of the Poisson we were working with was

  for (i in 1:N)
    mu[i] <- intercept
      + sigmaMont * varmont[mont[i]]
      + sigmaYear * varyear[year[i]]
      + sigmaERR * inderr[i];

which then feeds into

  y ~ poisson_log(mu);

aka

  y ~ poisson(exp(mu));

And we expect mu on the scale of 17 here because that's
roughly the mean of the data y.  Are you suggesting:

   mu[i] <- 17 * (intercept
      + sigmaMont * varmont[mont[i]]
      + sigmaYear * varyear[year[i]]
      + sigmaERR * inderr[i]);

or just

   mu[i] <- 17 * intercept
      + sigmaMont * varmont[mont[i]]
      + sigmaYear * varyear[year[i]]
      + sigmaERR * inderr[i];

or something else entirely?

Neither one actually worked with this problem that lme4 can fit
submitted by atzap on the list.  At least not in the way I tried it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, September 15, 2015 at 2:39:29 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I would not recommend 2, because I don't think you can easily fake
> a hard constraint with a soft constraint.
>
> The problem for (1) isn't so much that you need a Jacobian with this transform
>
> >   x[i,1] <- (y[i] - a[i, 2] x[i, 2] - a[i, 3] x[i, 3]) / a[i, 1];
>
> but rather that it's that you're trying to provide three distributions for
> x[i,1:3] on what are effectively two variables, x[i,2:3] and a funciton of them.
> So you need to work out what the implications are.  It's like you're doing
> something like this:
>
>   y[1] ~ foo(...);
>   y[2] ~ foo(...);
>   y[1] + y[2] ~ foo(...);
>
> It's much easier to work with a model conceptually if you can imagine
> the generative process leading to the data.
>

Perhaps, but I believe that the above type of model is a perfectly valid declarative model. After some recent discussions here I posted to my blog a variety of posts on declarative vs generative bayesian models.

http://models.street-artists.org/?s=declarative

I'd be interested to hear your thoughts Bob, as you may have some experience with declarative vs imperative programming, and I think the analogy is quite good.

I'd be very interested to hear what a run of Geoff's model declared as in his (1) does. The big issue as I see it is only that he may have difficulty with sampling because of the possibility for diff to be negative and so samples to be rejected as falling off the edge of the world... Depending on his data, this might only be a theoretical problem and not a practical one.

As for the need for a jacobian with the diff statement, I've managed to convince myself that no jacobian is needed in this statement, as it's a statement of the probability associated to a transformed data point conditional on the values of the parameters. It's not even sensible to talk about the jacobian because the transform takes one data value and 5 parameters to a new "transformed data" value. Presumably if the parameters are correct then the transformed data value is in the high probability region of the lognormal, and if they're incorrect then the transformed value is NOT in the high probability region, and so the probability of those parameters is highly downweighted, thereby giving you the posterior inference you want.

After drinking the full blown Cox Theorem version of Bayesianism, it seems one is pretty free to use declarative probabilistic statements in modeling.

messages.body_plain:
This one's way out of my comfort zone in terms of modeling.
I hope someone else can help on details.

You do want to get all your parameters on the same scale to
the extent possible.  Adaptation will help with this, but it's
not perfect.  You can try running longer warmup periods (perhaps
starting from a lower stepsize and targeting a higher adapt_delta
[acceptance rate]).

There is a log_mix function that will simplify your transformed
parameters considerably.  And given that lp_2 doesn't show up
in the model, that would be better defined in the generated
quantities block as a local variable so you don't need to write
it all out.

Usually you care about expectations, so don't need to actually
sample from the Bernoulli --- all you need to know about it can
be recovered from prob_lp_2.  Neat use of softmax in the generated
quantities block, by the way --- I always just did that by hand,
but your way is much better for computing prob_lp_2.

- Bob

>
> The model fits well when I fit only the additive terms f(t) + f(a), or when I fit only the bivariate function f(t,a), but when I fit the additive model g(t,a) = f(t) + f(a) + f(t,a) the step size becomes very very small, it reaches maximum tree depth, and n_divergent is high. I suspect that the problem may be related to the variance parameter associated with f(t,a) is much smaller than the variance on f(t) and f(a).
>
> The likelihood for the real data is more complicated and computationally expensive, but for the purposes of exploring the model structure I’ve created a simple Poisson likelihood (attached). I’ve parameterized the model in two ways (1) parameterizing the values of the response g(t,a) and applying linear transformations to recover the underlying f(t), f(a), f(t,a), and (2) directly parameterizing f(t), f(a), and f(t,a) [with sum-to-zero constraints for identifiability].

But when I simulate more realistic data, such that the variation in f(t,a) is much less than in f(t) and f(a) dimensions, I get much the same as with the real data -- very small step size, and poor convergence. I’m wondering if anyone has advice for better parameterization of the model? (Or if I’ve done something obviously silly...)

Andrew and Michael and Ben are the three you really want on this case.

As to the Jacobian calculation, the function maps (x[i,2], x[i,3], y[i])
to (x[i,2], x[i,3], x[i,1]), so you can just work it out (I put it in
that order to make sure the Jacobian's triangular and has an easy determinant).
I think you're right here that the Jacobian term drops out in Stan (but
you should check that --- my Jacobian calcs are error prone without extensive
unit testing).

As to the blog, I don't believe there are "declarative" programming
languages in practice.  In order to program Prolog well (as outlined,
for instance, in O'Keefe's awesome book, The Craft of Prolog), you have
to know how it's evaluated.  If you don't, you'll get infinite loops at
worst, and inefficient programs at best.  Order matters in practice, if not in theory,
because evaluation is depth first.  Same for SQL --- you need to show the plan
in order to evaluate how good a program you get from your code.

The proof for Prolog is really simple.  You code up an array with
binary search access --- it's where the log term comes from.  In practice,
though, things are much worse in that some algorithms are nearly impossible
to convert to even moderately efficient Prolog (all that theory ignores
important little facts like memory locality and garbage collection overhead).

This used to be my bread and butter --- computation theory and logic programming :-)
I even wrote a book on the topic.

I was expecting the analogy to be that the generative model was declarative.
The truly declarative approach here, in my opinion, is laying out the joint
density.  The generative approach is one way to do that, the imperative approach
is another, but in both cases, at least in Stan, all you're doing is defining
the joint density.

I put an edited form of these comments on the blog, or I should say, put them
into the moderation queue.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Heavy tailed distributions (eg Cauchy) and fast sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Quick question regarding STAN and sampling from heavy tailed distributions.

I know that this is difficult for the sampler because of the non-Euclidean geometry, and that there are suggested workarounds (eg inverse transform sampling for Cauchy, mixture of normals for t distribution - although I'm not clear on whether on is generally better or not).

Suppose I have a linear regression model with coefficients {beta} and regressors {x}, and I put a Cauchy prior on the regression coefficients ie beta[i] ~ Cauchy(0, tau) for some tau.

As the number of data points increases, should not the regression coefficients become ~ normally distributed (by the central limit theorem) and therefore the STAN sampler should not have any problems exploring the posterior?  In this scenario, do you need to worry about reparameterising the beta[i] priors (or could this even make things worse)?

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, September 23, 2015 at 5:26:37 PM UTC-7, Daniel Lakeland wrote:

>
> at least, that's how I read it. I admit to being a little distracted at the moment, so hopefully Geoff will delve deeper to confirm as needed.
>
>

My small child distraction is itself distracted, so I thought I might help clarify my thinking here:

If you know the value of x[i,2], x[i,3], and the a[i,j] values etc, then you can calculate x[i,1] and it's exactly equal to "diff".

Taking the full Cox/Bayes view of bayesian inference, where the probability values are relative credibility measures, you can then ask:

How credible is it that the x[i,2], x[i,3], and a[i,j] values really are what the sampler is telling me they currently are, given the observed y value? Well, it's more or less credible based on not what the value of y is, but what the value of "diff" is, which is a function of y and the other parameters. And the relative credibility of the diff values is given by the lognormal density function, hence

diff ~ lognormal(...)

in the end, as Bob says, you wind up defining a density over the parameters, and you can work out what it is, but it's somewhat more complicated than usual.

So, although it's not *generative* because it doesn't specify that "y" is a sample from some surrogate mathematical probability density (ie. it doesn't have y ~ foo_density(...)), it is a meaningful bayesian model in the same way that ABC models are meaningful bayesian models, even though the accept/reject criterion is not a generative one either.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Heavy tailed distributions (eg Cauchy) and fast sampling
messages.body_plain:
> I know that this is difficult for the sampler because of the non-Euclidean geometry, and that there are suggested workarounds (eg inverse transform sampling for Cauchy, mixture of normals for t distribution - although I'm not clear on whether on is generally better or not).

Clarification — the heaviness of Cauchy tails has nothing to do with wether or
not the sample space has a Euclidean geometry.  The real problem is that
the heavy-tailed distributions yield heavy-tailed probability densities when
the sample space is Euclidean, and it’s the heavy-tailed density that causes
problems.

An important consequence of this more careful perspective — changing
parameters does not change the target distribution but can change the
density.  Which is why the strategies you mention can improve sampling
without changing the problem.

> Suppose I have a linear regression model with coefficients {beta} and regressors {x}, and I put a Cauchy prior on the regression coefficients ie beta[i] ~ Cauchy(0, tau) for some tau.
>
> As the number of data points increases, should not the regression coefficients become ~ normally distributed (by the central limit theorem) and therefore the STAN sampler should not have any problems exploring the posterior?  In this scenario, do you need to worry about reparameterising the beta[i] priors (or could this even make things worse)?

It depends on how much data you have.  The more data the better
behaved the target distribution will be, but there’s no way to judge
that a priori as it will be very sensitive to your exact data.

That said, we typically recommend Gaussian priors for regression
coefficients and save Cauchy priors for regression standard
deviation.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.body_plain:
Whaaaaaaaaa?

I can’t follow this discussion at all, but let me try to clarify a few points that have come up.

First — the Cox/Jaynes perspective has absolutely no impact on modeling. It’s just an (incomplete)
motivation for why we can always place inductive learning into a probabilistic framework.  For more
details on the incompleteness of Cox/Jaynes in general state spaces see http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.06597.

Second — there’s nothing “generative” or “imperative” about our posterior distributions.  If
we had an imperative description of the posterior then we wouldn’t need HMC — we’d just
use ancestral sampling to get exact samples!  It is far more accurate to say that posterior
distributions in Stan are “declarative” in that the user declares a posterior (via a density)
and the code draws samples without the user having to specify how samples are drawn.
This is _always_ how Stan works.

The confusion arises because we advocate thinking generatively when building up a
_likelihood_.  Users typically have strong information about how the data were
generated, so this generative perspective makes it easier to build up robust likelihoods
representative of the true underlying process.  But, again, in Stan you don’t have to
specify a target distribution as prior + generative likelihood.  You can specify whatever
you want provided it is a self-consistent probability density.  We just find that prior +
generative likelihood is the easiest way to guarantee such a valid density.

Finally — another obfuscating aspect here is the difference between probability distributions
(measures) verses probability densities.  Densities are a parameterization-dependent
representation of a distribution, and the Jacobian comes around when comparing densities
from different parameterizations.  Jacobians arise in this example because you’re trying
to specify densities for parameterizations that are inconsistent with the parameterizations
assumed by the Stan probability densities.  Ultimately, if x ~ some_distribution then we
don’t know the distribution for f(x) so you have to define that yourself.  If you get it wrong
then you’ve specified a density for a different probability distribution!

>
> My small child distraction is itself distracted, so I thought I might help clarify my thinking here:
>
> If you know the value of x[i,2], x[i,3], and the a[i,j] values etc, then you can calculate x[i,1] and it's exactly equal to "diff".
>
> Taking the full Cox/Bayes view of bayesian inference, where the probability values are relative credibility measures, you can then ask:
>
> How credible is it that the x[i,2], x[i,3], and a[i,j] values really are what the sampler is telling me they currently are, given the observed y value? Well, it's more or less credible based on not what the value of y is, but what the value of "diff" is, which is a function of y and the other parameters. And the relative credibility of the diff values is given by the lognormal density function, hence
>
> diff ~ lognormal(...)
>
> in the end, as Bob says, you wind up defining a density over the parameters, and you can work out what it is, but it's somewhat more complicated than usual.
>
> So, although it's not *generative* because it doesn't specify that "y" is a sample from some surrogate mathematical probability density (ie. it doesn't have y ~ foo_density(...)), it is a meaningful bayesian model in the same way that ABC models are meaningful bayesian models, even though the accept/reject criterion is not a generative one either.
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks everyone for chiming in!

@ Michael:
I was indeed trying to scale the parameter, not the data. More specifically,
I was looking for a way to keep all parameters roughly on the same scale,
because my understanding was that this makes it easier to find a good step size
during adaption of the HMC algorithm. But I am not sure, because my understanding of HMC is superficial.

I agree that the issue I am trying to address is a different thing that what you were thinking about.
Sorry if my description was unclear.

@ Andrew and Bob:
As Andrew noted, in my initial proposal I did not take
into account that I used neg_binomial_2_log.
I think the log is crucial, and I don't think the last two
proposals Bob made take this into account.
The first formula of course works, but it could still
have the problem that the intercept parameter is
orders of magnitude larger than the other parameters.

Here is now one hopefully correct way to set the model up such
that all parameters have a similar order of magnitude:

When I have count data y with a mean of around m
and use a regression approach to calculate log_mu = x*beta,
(where log_mu = log(mean_of_the_Poisson)
and x includes an intercept regressor)

then one would simply write
y ~ poisson(exp(log_mu) + m)

Does this make sense?

If I remember correctly, it is preferable to use
y ~ poisson_log(log_mu) instead of y ~ poisson(mu).

But I don't know how to do a simple addition on the log scale.

Please also tell me if it actually does not matter when the parameters
have different orders of magnitude....

Best - Guido

On Thursday, September 24, 2015 at 1:46:25 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Whaaaaaaaaa?
>
> I can’t follow this discussion at all, but let me try to clarify a few points that have come up.
>
> First — the Cox/Jaynes perspective has absolutely no impact on modeling.

Well, I see we are in complete disagreement here. In particular the Cox perspective gives motivation for the MEANING of a distribution, and so it has EVERYTHING to do with modeling, since modeling is about creating a meaningful connection between the world and some mathematical statements. The Cox perspective tells you what you can put a distribution on (basically anything quantifiable), and what that distribution means (a degree of plausibility, not a relative frequency of occurrence, in particular, we need not match the empirical frequency of data points to the distribution function).

On the other hand, I completely agree with you when it comes to implementing a sampler. After the modeling, the mathematics is the mathematics. And Stan's whole purpose is to create a machine that explicitly connects the Bayesian plausibility measures to frequency measures in the output of Stan. The "problem" here is that Stan makes it so easy to connect the model to the code that the difference is sometimes hard to see  (that's a compliment to you all!)

>Second — there’s nothing “generative” or “imperative” about our posterior distributions.

There are however "generative" vs "declarative" methods of modeling. This discussion is about the step before you write down a Stan model, or rather, because Stan makes it so easy to translate ideas into code, it winds up looking more like interpreting the meaning (in terms of what it implies for the world) of Stan statements.

The confusion arises because we advocate thinking generatively when building up a
_likelihood_.  Users typically have strong information about how the data were
generated, so this generative perspective makes it easier to build up robust likelihoods
representative of the true underlying process.  But, again, in Stan you don’t have to
specify a target distribution as prior + generative likelihood.  You can specify whatever

you want provided it is a self-consistent probability density.

Yes, this is exactly the case. Here I'm arguing thinking about Stan statements as declarative statements which are valid Bayesian modeling statements (they are meaningful for describing the real-world process) even though they **don't define a likelihood** (at least, they don't define a likelihood based on data coming from an iid sampling process). They do, however, define a weighting function for the prior which acts like a likelihood (it downweights the parameter values which are inconsistent with the probabilistic statement of fact). From the Cox perspective, this is a perfectly natural thing to do, whereas from other perspectives of probability, it's meaningless because probability = frequency of occurrence, so you'd have to write statements of the form data ~ my_distribution because that's got a meaningful connection to frequencies.

In this case, Geoff's model (1) may well run just fine even though the statement

diff ~ lognormal(...)

doesn't define the usual type of iid likelihood.

It's worth coding the model and trying it out before going down other roads, because the only thing "wrong" with it is that it might fall off the edge of the world, when diff becomes negative. but that might not happen given his data and priors.

I hope that clarifies my position here. And please note: I'm just trying to help Geoff and others get something both meaningful and useful.

No.  No it’s not.

Cox-Jaynes tells you that uncertainty of logical statements is equivalent to Komologorov
measure theory (up to the aforementioned technical details that are still somewhat
unresolved).  At that point any learning has to be consistent with those rules of measure
theory and there is a huge wealth of literature showing that Bayes theorem (prior + likelihood)
is the only self-consistent means of updating an initial distribution with data.  The road
to alternative parameter updates is paved with fuzzy sets.

You can specify whatever distribution you want in Stan and provided it admits a smooth
density with respect to the Lebesgue measure corresponding to the given parameterization
then Stan will draw samples (hopefully successfully).  But unless that posterior arises from
a proper (not necessarily unique) prior + likelihood breakdown then it will not be a well-defined
inference procedure.  Again, we don’t enforce this but it also means that you’re on your own
when it comes to interpreting the results.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.body_plain:
I really like this part:

> ... posterior

> distributions in Stan are “declarative” in that the user declares a posterior (via a density)
> and the code draws samples without the user having to specify how samples are drawn.
> This is _always_ how Stan works.
>

> ... we advocate thinking generatively when building up a

> _likelihood_.  Users typically have strong information about how the data were
> generated, so this generative perspective makes it easier to build up robust likelihoods
> representative of the true underlying process.

For me, it's this second step of building up reasonable likelihoods
(and priors) and then being able to do inference with them that makes Bayesian
modeling so attractive.  Being able to account for how the data came
about both in terms of the underlying process (science) and the
measurement is critical.  Basically what Andrew outlines in the first
bit of the first chapter of Bayesian Data Analysis.

> But, again, in Stan you don’t have to
> specify a target distribution as prior + generative likelihood.  You can specify whatever
> you want provided it is a self-consistent probability density.  We just find that prior +
> generative likelihood is the easiest way to guarantee such a valid density.

We need to somehow make that clearer.  I've been trying
in talks to emphasize how the sampling notation is just
a syntactic shorthand.

- Bob

> On Sep 24, 2015, at 10:01 AM, Tamas Papp <tkp...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thu, Sep 24 2015, Daniel Lakeland <dlak...@street-artists.org> wrote:
>
>> The confusion arises because we advocate thinking generatively when
>> building up a _likelihood_.  Users typically have strong information
>> about how the data were generated, so this generative perspective
>> makes it easier to build up robust likelihoods representative of the
>> true underlying process.  But, again, in Stan you don’t have to
>
> The only time I have strong information about how my data was generated
> is when I simulate said data myself for testing some code.
>
> I don't know about other fields, but in social sciences such notions of
> "strong information" about the DGP are rapidly shipwrecked by the
> laughter of the gods.

Maybe we mean something different by "strong" here.  From Andrew
et al.'s work on voting, there are modeling decisions such as which
demographic information to include (age, sex, education, income,
state of residence, etc.), where to include multilevel factors (effect
of income might vary by state of residence and have a correlated slope
and intercept), when to include time-series data (maybe voting varies
over time based on what politics was like when you came of age in
addition to the age trend itself), when to include interactions (interaction
of income and education), and so on.

Another example is Aki's take on the birthday problem (what calendar day
kids are born on).  It's largely a social issue for humans, so Aki took
into account seasonal effects, day of week effects, special holiday effects,
a general historical trend, and so on).

In both cases, this isn't so much generative as it is regression based
(what a machine learning person would call "discriminative" in contrast
to "generative", to which Andrew objects for reasons explained in BDA [short
answer is that you can and should think of the whole model as generative
with the predictor model marginalized out due to an independence assumption]).

The main motivation for building Stan was that there were such intuitions
that Andrew et al. had that couldn't be fit in other software.
(And they're still not super easy to fit in Stan, but it's possible.)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Sep 24, 2015, at 6:48 AM, Guido Biele <guido...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks everyone for chiming in!
>
> @ Michael:
> I was indeed trying to scale the parameter, not the data. More specifically,
> I was looking for a way to keep all parameters roughly on the same scale,
> because my understanding was that this makes it easier to find a good step size
> during adaption of the HMC algorithm. But I am not sure, because my understanding of HMC is superficial.
>
> I agree that the issue I am trying to address is a different thing that what you were thinking about.
> Sorry if my description was unclear.
>
> @ Andrew and Bob:
> As Andrew noted, in my initial proposal I did not take
> into account that I used neg_binomial_2_log.
> I think the log is crucial, and I don't think the last two
> proposals Bob made take this into account.
> The first formula of course works, but it could still
> have the problem that the intercept parameter is
> orders of magnitude larger than the other parameters.
>
> Here is now one hopefully correct way to set the model up such
> that all parameters have a similar order of magnitude:
>
> When I have count data y with a mean of around m
> and use a regression approach to calculate log_mu = x*beta,
> (where log_mu = log(mean_of_the_Poisson)
> and x includes an intercept regressor)
>
> then one would simply write
> y ~ poisson(exp(log_mu) + m)
>
> Does this make sense?
>
> If I remember correctly, it is preferable to use
> y ~ poisson_log(log_mu) instead of y ~ poisson(mu).

If you have mu on the log scale (as in most GLMs), then that's
right.  But if your parameter is mu, you do not want to do this:

  y ~ poisson_log(log(mu))

just so you can use poisson_log.

> But I don't know how to do a simple addition on the log scale.

log_sum_exp() does just that.

If you have log(a) and log(b), and want to compute log(a + b), then

  log_sum_exp(log(a), log(b))

    = log(exp(log(a)), exp(log(b)))

    = log(a + b)

> Please also tell me if it actually does not matter when the parameters
> have different orders of magnitude....

It can matter.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sum of lognormals?
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, September 24, 2015 at 8:50:33 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> No.  No it’s not.
>
> Cox-Jaynes tells you that uncertainty of logical statements is equivalent to Komologorov
> measure theory (up to the aforementioned technical details that are still somewhat
> unresolved).  At that point any learning has to be consistent with those rules of measure
> theory and there is a huge wealth of literature showing that Bayes theorem (prior + likelihood)
> is the only self-consistent means of updating an initial distribution with data.

I disagree, ABC is a hugely effective procedure in some circumstances, but it doesn't involve a likelihood in which data is the result of IID draws from a distribution, yet the typical accept-reject method can be thought of as updating a prior with the additional probabilistic information assigned as:

distance(summary(fake_data(parameters)),summary(real_data)) ~ uniform(0,epsilon)

for some complicated function "summary" and some complicated function "fake_data" (often a black box physical simulator) and some choice of distance function.

After the model is specified, measure theory takes over. So if you're interested in using the above ABC statement, but you want to compute with a slightly different distance function that's easier to calculate, you'll need to jacobian transform the uniform density for example...

But before the model is specified we're talking a modeling process, there is rarely one true model. So what's important is how we choose and interpret models. One GREAT way to choose models is to use a generative formalism to describe them, but it's not the only way.

I think to avoid talking past each other it's probably important here to define what is meant by a likelihood, and the usual definition is p(data | parameters) and we have to assign that, it's not an automatic thing you can prove from first principles. And, there's no reason to think that you need to say express that in terms of IID sampling, or restrict yourself to the data space. why not work in some kind of complicated distance between the summaries of the generated simulations and the data?

p(distance(summary(fake_data(parameters)),summary(real_data)) | parameters) ??? if you know the answer to what the plausible values are for that expression then you can define a density over that distance which expresses the plausibility, and get a proper (proper in a Cox/Jaynes interpretation) posterior for parameters.

Perhaps you'd just include this in "likelihoods" so we may be talking past each other based on definition of what is meant by "likelihood".

Or perhaps you disagree that assigning a distribution to distance(summary(fake_data(parameters)),summary(real_data)) is a valid thing to do. I would be very interested to clarify.

On Thursday, September 24, 2015 at 1:08:01 PM UTC-7, Daniel Lakeland wrote:
>
>
> On Thursday, September 24, 2015 at 8:50:33 AM UTC-7, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >
> > No.  No it’s not.
> >
> > Cox-Jaynes tells you that uncertainty of logical statements is equivalent to Komologorov
> > measure theory (up to the aforementioned technical details that are still somewhat
> > unresolved).  At that point any learning has to be consistent with those rules of measure
> > theory and there is a huge wealth of literature showing that Bayes theorem (prior + likelihood)
> > is the only self-consistent means of updating an initial distribution with data.
>

Another way to put my point is that measure theory doesn't get to tell you what you are going to model. It only gets to tell you *after* you specify the model, what you can do with it while keeping it invariant and logically consistent. If you have some data that you don't know much about, but you know a lot about some function of that data conditional on some values of some parameters, you can model that function.

That's exactly what Geoff's model (1) does. it assigns plausibilities to an expression "diff" which according to him under his modeling assumptions and conditional on the proper values of the parameters, looks like a number pulled from a lognormal distribution. This doesn't violate any rules of logic or measure theory, it is just a choice to model something other than the observed data point. Since the observed data point is always a function of some other stuff anyway (position of a needle on a gauge is a function of a current and a spring constant and some geometry and whatnot) this should be pretty obvious.

messages.body_plain:
This mailing list and especially this thread are probably
not the best venue for discussing the theory of probability
modeling.  Let me just sum up what Stan does so that doesn't
get lost in all of this discussion.

Stan only requires you to define a the log of p(theta|y)
where p(theta|y) is your posterior up to a proportion.
The requirements are that it be differentiable in order
for HMC to work, have support on its declared constraints
for Stan to work, be defined in our language, so that we
can compute derivatives, and to be proper (finite integral).
Sometimes even with all this, the geometry will be too difficult
to adapt to or sample from, which will show up in the
convergence diagnostics.

You can define p(theta|y) any way you want.  A Bayesian
would often define the posterior in terms of a likelihood
and prior via Bayes's rule as

   p(theta | y)  propto  p(y | theta) p(theta)

For a Bayesian, nothing requires p(y | theta) to involve
a vector of data y that is i.i.d.  It can be anything.

If you prefer penalized likelihoods and point estimation, you can think
of a model as defining a log penalized likelihood, as in

  LL_penalized(y | theta) =  log p(y | theta) + pen_fun(theta)

where pen_fun(theta) is some penalty function.  Then the optimizers
will maximize this to find the penalized MLE.

- Bob

messages.subject: fitting binomial nonlinear model in Stan question
messages.subject_clean: fitting binomial nonlinear model in Stan question
messages.body_plain:
Several things here:

(1) y and n should be declared as integer array and not vectors (which contain real numbers). So you need int y[N] and likewise for n.

(2) pi should be declared in the transformed parameters block since it is a deterministic function of parameters. It also needs to have N elements, one for each value of conc. The statement assigning a value to pi that you have in the model block also should move to transformed parameters as a loop (I don't think exp is vectorized yet, but I might be wrong).

That should get the model running. However, you can and should avoid all of (2) by using y~binomial_logit(n, beta[1]*(conc - beta[2])), which does it all on the logit scale for you so you don't need to do the transformation yourself.

I hope that helps. If any of that doesn't make sense let me know.

messages.body_plain:
Hi. I am very interested in getting this to work. The closest I'm aware of is probably the Kronecker GP stuff I've been working on--if you're happy with gridding up your counts, you can approximate an LGCP with a GP with Poisson observation model and use Kronecker (or FFT) for scalability [see my ICML paper <http://jmlr.org/proceedings/papers/v37/flaxman15.html>, not Stan though]--but I did indeed run into issues with the non Gaussian observation model in Stan. Happy to share code in any case... And also this was before ADVI was around so that might help!

What's the scale of your data / observation window? Had you thought about how you'd like to set it up, e.g. using a grid as I did (following Diggle et al), or more like the sigmoidal idea [Adams 2009] or uniformization [Teh <http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~teh/research/compstats/RaoTeh2011b.pdf> 2011]. I haven't thought yet about how we might implement those in Stan, but I'd be happy to discuss more.

Best,
Seth

messages.subject: HMC + Stan for data driven Markov Chains
messages.subject_clean: HMC + Stan for data driven Markov Chains
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I am working on indoor semantic segmentation. I would like to implement an approach in paper "Sampling bedrooms", by Luca Del Pero, Jinyan Guan, Ernesto Brau, Joseph Schlecht, Kobus Barnard, CVPR 2011 <http://kobus.ca/research/publications/11/CVPR-11-1958.pdf>.

This approach optimizes the camera parameters and room dimensions given a single image.
The posterior probability function matches the image edges with the edges of the model generated by given set of camera parameters and bedroom dimensions.
They use Hamiltonian Markov chain with leap frog discretization.

I am looking a way to use STAN library to solve this problem more efficiently. What I cannot figure out is how to generate the data block for this problem in STAN.

Apparently the data here is the image edge points.
I have not seen any example in the documentation which addresses computer vision problem.

Can anyone one point me to the right direction/documentation/example?

Best
Ishrat

>
> This approach optimizes the camera parameters and room dimensions given a single image.
> The posterior probability function matches the image edges with the edges of the model generated by given set of camera parameters and bedroom dimensions.
> They use Hamiltonian Markov chain with leap frog discretization.
>
> I am looking a way to use STAN library to solve this problem more efficiently. What I cannot figure out is how to generate the data block for this problem in STAN.
>
> Apparently the data here is the image edge points.
> I have not seen any example in the documentation which addresses computer vision problem.
>
> Can anyone one point me to the right direction/documentation/example?

I'm going to go out on a limb here, as I'm not a Stan developer, but I kind of doubt you'll be able to do computer vision problems in Stan in a reasonable amount of coding time.

There is no "image" datatype in Stan, and if you instead convert the images to arrays of integers or real numbers then you'll have to implement image processing code from scratch in the Stan language, or bolted on in C++ or something. I'm not saying it CAN'T be done, but it's not obvious that it's the right way to go.

That being said,  perhaps you can first pre-process your images to get some kind of reduced data sets, and then run a Stan model on those reduced data sets, and then use the Stan output to inform your computer vision processing. That seems like a reasonable technique. The pre-processing step might be some kind of edge detection. This is a non-trivial problem, so if you can maybe think hard on it and then ask a more targeted question I suspect people can give more help.

messages.body_plain:
See below.

> On Sep 24, 2015, at 2:58 PM, Ian <ian.va...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> I am trying to fit a nonlinear model in which the stochastic component is a bernoulli random variable:
>      y ~ bernoulli(n, pi)
>
> and the stochastic component is non-linear
>
>     pi = exp(beta1*(conc - beta2)/(1 +exp(beta1*(conc - beta2) ))
>
> The parameters being beta1 and beta2. My data looks like this:
>   Obs j conc  n  y
> 1   1 1 50.1 48 48
> 2   2 2 40.7 50 47
> 3   3 3 30.2 49 47
> 4   4 4 20.4 48 34
> 5   5 5 10.0 48 18
> 6   6 6  5.1 49 16
>
>
>
>  I am struggling to fit this model in Stan. Here's my attempt:
>
> model<-"data {
> int<lower=0> N;
> vector[N] y;
> vector[N] conc;
> vector[N] n;
> }
> parameters {
> vector[2] beta;
> real<lower=0, upper=1> pi;
> }
> model {
> y ~ binomial(n, pi);
> pi <- exp(beta[1]*(conc - beta[2])/(1 +exp(beta[1]*(conc - beta[2]) ));
> }"
>

1.  You can't assign to parameters like pi, so it needs to be a local.

2.  You need to define pi before you use it.

3.  But you don't need any of that in Stan.

4.  y needs to be declared as an array of integers because binomials
use count data and vectors are continuous data by definition in Stan.
I don't know if n is count, too, in which case it should also be an integer.

data {
  int y[N];
  ...
parameters {
  vector[2] beta;
}
model {
  real pi;

  pi <- exp(beta[1]*(conc - beta[2])/(1 +exp(beta[1]*(conc - beta[2]) ));

  y ~ binomial(n, pi);

  beta ~ ???
}

5.  You probably want some kind of prior on beta.  It's not necessary if
the posterior's proper, but it's usually a good idea.

- Bob

messages.subject: Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.subject_clean: Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a relatively simple Poisson regression problem with n=700, and about 20 regressors (so around 20 regression coefficients).

The adaptation period is, I think, unexpectedly slow, at around one sample per few seconds..

If I start with inits=0,  the chain basically doesn't move for the first few hundred iterations, then moves thereafter.  If I start with init = the parameters from the mode found by the optimiser, the rate of sampling is relatively constant.

After looking at the sampler parameters, max_treedepth is hit the whole way through the first hundreds of iterations.  Increasing max_treedepth up to 12 in accordance with the suggestion in the manual just makes the sampling take a lot longer (tree depth keeps hitting 12).

After adaptation for n=500 iterations (250 warmup and 250 sampling), the effective sample sizes for the parameters are quite high however - often near 250.

I suspect that the problem may be due to some of my regressors.  Groups of regressors unavoidably define a simplex (ie the sum of each of the regressors in a particular group is one).  In fact, I omit one of the regressors from the simplex due to the linear dependence (eg if regressors 1 through 8 define a simplex, then I only use 1 through 7 in the model in order to avoid the degeneracy).  For example, one of my regressors is the percentage of people in a particular age group, eg ages 0-17, 18-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, and 80+.  In this context I omit the "80+" group to avoid the total degeneracy.

In order to mitigate the potential degeneracy issue and to implement shrinkage, I have put a hierarchical prior on each of the simplex-like groups of regressors with a zero mean (eg age[i] ~ normal(0, sig_age)  in the example above), and I have put a vaguely informative prior on sig_age.

There are a number of possible other causes:
Scale of regressors (and therefore potential scale of regression coefficients) does vary somewhat - by about 3 orders of magnitude
I have not used the Matt trick - but if I try removing the hierarchical priors (sig_age in the example above) the speed is not significantly affected, so perhaps this is not the cause
Things I have tried:
I have vectorised all the sampling statements, so this isn't the issue.
I have tried using a dense mass matrix, and this doesn't seem to make any significant difference.

My question is:  has anyone encountered behaviour like this, and do you have any solutions?  I cannot avoid the use of simplex regressors in this case, but in some cases could amalgamate the groups (but do not wish to do so if I can avoid it).

I appreciate that maybe I just have to live with the slow sampling - perhaps Stan is behaving as expected.

Thoughts appreciated about where my efforts in optimising the model are best spent.

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, just a quick guess:  there is typically overdispersion and Poisson regression can run slowly then becuase it’s trying too hard to fit the data.  You could try overdispersed.
A

> On Sep 26, 2015, at 5:35 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Hi all,
>
> I have a relatively simple Poisson regression problem with n=700, and about 20 regressors (so around 20 regression coefficients).
>
> The adaptation period is, I think, unexpectedly slow, at around one sample per few seconds..
>
> If I start with inits=0,  the chain basically doesn't move for the first few hundred iterations, then moves thereafter.  If I start with init = the parameters from the mode found by the optimiser, the rate of sampling is relatively constant.
>
> After looking at the sampler parameters, max_treedepth is hit the whole way through the first hundreds of iterations.  Increasing max_treedepth up to 12 in accordance with the suggestion in the manual just makes the sampling take a lot longer (tree depth keeps hitting 12).
>
> After adaptation for n=500 iterations (250 warmup and 250 sampling), the effective sample sizes for the parameters are quite high however - often near 250.
>
> I suspect that the problem may be due to some of my regressors.  Groups of regressors unavoidably define a simplex (ie the sum of each of the regressors in a particular group is one).  In fact, I omit one of the regressors from the simplex due to the linear dependence (eg if regressors 1 through 8 define a simplex, then I only use 1 through 7 in the model in order to avoid the degeneracy).  For example, one of my regressors is the percentage of people in a particular age group, eg ages 0-17, 18-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, and 80+.  In this context I omit the "80+" group to avoid the total degeneracy.
>
> In order to mitigate the potential degeneracy issue and to implement shrinkage, I have put a hierarchical prior on each of the simplex-like groups of regressors with a zero mean (eg age[i] ~ normal(0, sig_age)  in the example above), and I have put a vaguely informative prior on sig_age.
>
> There are a number of possible other causes:
> Scale of regressors (and therefore potential scale of regression coefficients) does vary somewhat - by about 3 orders of magnitude
> I have not used the Matt trick - but if I try removing the hierarchical priors (sig_age in the example above) the speed is not significantly affected, so perhaps this is not the cause
> Things I have tried:
> I have vectorised all the sampling statements, so this isn't the issue.
> I have tried using a dense mass matrix, and this doesn't seem to make any significant difference.
>
> My question is:  has anyone encountered behaviour like this, and do you have any solutions?  I cannot avoid the use of simplex regressors in this case, but in some cases could amalgamate the groups (but do not wish to do so if I can avoid it).
>
> I appreciate that maybe I just have to live with the slow sampling - perhaps Stan is behaving as expected.
>
> Thoughts appreciated about where my efforts in optimising the model are best spent.
>
> Thanks in advance!
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Sometimes fitting a more general model can be faster.  I'd be surprised if
that were the case with the Poisson --- usually we have more trouble
estimating the overdispersion.

Scale variation of several orders of magnitude essentially introduces
stiffness into Stan's ODE solver --- it can't go too fast in the most
highly constrained dimension.

The problem is that it needs to learn which dimension that is during
warmup, which would explain why things are OK after warmup.  If there's a
way you could rescale, that'd probably help a lot.

You can take a look at the scaling parameters after the run to see what
warmup did.

Tree depth of 10 is 1024 log probability and gradient evals per iteration,
and depth 12 is 4 times that many.  That's the main reason it's going to
be slow.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
To unask the last question, the lgamma function is used for
the Poisson, but it's only calculated if you call poisson_log(...)
as a function.  If you use sampling notation, it will be a constant
and be dropped.

When log factorials are needed, we calculate them using the lgamma function
from Boost:

  http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_59_0/libs/math/doc/html/math_toolkit/sf_gamma/lgamma.html

and digamma and trigamma for derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: Multinomial distribution & regression
messages.subject_clean: Multinomial distribution & regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to run a regression model on data that falls into three classes, with a number of covariates. Since the aim of the project is to find the probability of being in class 1, 2 or 3 giving covariates (and the effect of covariates on the probability), I thought it could be done using a simple multinomial regression model. Due to the very large number of data points I tried to count how many samples fall into each combination of class and covariates (I read on these forums that sampling can be faster using aggregated groups instead of individual samples for very large data sets). Also, I am not even sure if this is proper to do, so please correct me if I am going on a wild goose chase. Anywho, I ran into the problem that Stans implementation of the Multinomial distribution explicitly calculates the number N from the input vector y, and it cannot be given as an argument. I have tried looking a bit around on the forums, but either nothing is here or I am using a wrong search term.

I tried to implement it simply looping over the number of counts for each group, but that did not work well since the Multinomial distribution expects a vector. https://gist.github.com/demodw/ce5e4f7f7e83184049cc

Any advice is appreciated.

Cheers,
David

messages.body_plain:
If you have three outcomes and observe the second one
5 times for linear predictor theta[n], then you
can do something like this

  {
    int y[3];
    y[1] <- 0;
    y[2] <- 5;
    y[3] <- 0;

    y ~ categorical_logit(theta[n]);
  }

The open bracket creates a new scope so you can drop
this anywhere.  And the _logit means that you apply softmax
to get the usual categorical.

Alternatively, you can do this

  increment_log_prob(5 * categorical_logit_log(2, theta[n]));

The above should produce the same posterior as the following loop

  for (i in 1:count[n])
    y[n] ~ categorical_logit(theta[n]);

You can break a multinomial down this way, too.

We should really have a multinomial_logit to match categorical.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
An update on this:

I tried a negative binomial model, then just moved back to plain Poisson because the overdispersion in the data is not material
Placing somewhat more informative (but still pretty vague) priors seems to have helped
I am using a dense mass matrix and this helps, I think
I have used adapt_delta = 0.9, and this seems to help
Looking at the posterior for coefficients of the simplex regressor groups reveals very high correlations (r > 0.9), so this isn't exactly a very easy posterior to sample from.  Somewhat informative priors seem to have helped here, as per the suggestion in the manual for nearly-unidentified parameters.
It seems that simply a lot of warmup iterations are needed in order for Stan to learn the shape of the posterior.  With n=500 warmup iterations, max_treedepth is hit on most iterations early on, and progressively less later.  With larger numbers of warmup iterations the average number of leapfrog steps seems to decline, but there doesn't appear to be a 'eureka' moment where suddenly sampling quality drastically improves.

Unfortunately it just looks like I have a slow model.  My data re are constructed so that y=0 never appears, so I have to use a ~ poisson T[1,] statement, which is unfortunately not vectorised.

I'm happy that the model is working as intended, and the run time is long but not unmanageably.   Thanks for your help.

messages.body_plain:
I don't know how strict that truncation is (seems to be Poisson and
overdispersed and zero-inflated Poisson week), but rather than

  y[n] ~ poisson(alpha[n]) T[1,];

you could use

  (y[n] - 1) ~ poisson(alpha[n]);

Of course, the interpretation of alpha[n] is slightly different.

Alternatively, you can do the simple case of the Poisson by realizing
that the relevant CDF (1 - poisson_cdf(1, alpha[n])) can be coded
as (1 - exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n])).  Because you're going to need
that on the log scale, and it's a common operation, we have it built in
as

  log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]);

So you could code the whole model as

  y ~ poisson(alpha);
  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]));

Considerably uglier.  Now if the alpha[n] were all the same, it
could be made much more efficient.  As is, allowing the vectorization
now in the Poisson sampling statement shouldn't be too bad.

- Bob

> On Sep 28, 2015, at 4:16 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> An update on this:
>
> 	• I tried a negative binomial model, then just moved back to plain Poisson because the overdispersion in the data is not material
> 	• Placing somewhat more informative (but still pretty vague) priors seems to have helped
> 	• I am using a dense mass matrix and this helps, I think
> 	• I have used adapt_delta = 0.9, and this seems to help
> 	• Looking at the posterior for coefficients of the simplex regressor groups reveals very high correlations (r > 0.9), so this isn't exactly a very easy posterior to sample from.  Somewhat informative priors seem to have helped here, as per the suggestion in the manual for nearly-unidentified parameters.
> 	• It seems that simply a lot of warmup iterations are needed in order for Stan to learn the shape of the posterior.  With n=500 warmup iterations, max_treedepth is hit on most iterations early on, and progressively less later.  With larger numbers of warmup iterations the average number of leapfrog steps seems to decline, but there doesn't appear to be a 'eureka' moment where suddenly sampling quality drastically improves.
>
> Unfortunately it just looks like I have a slow model.  My data re are constructed so that y=0 never appears, so I have to use a ~ poisson T[1,] statement, which is unfortunately not vectorised.

messages.body_plain:
I am not quite sure I understand. I tried creating three individual arrays, one for each class, and then just running increment_log_prob three times (the model can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/9e69a07e24804afeb663), though I am not quite sure it behaves as I would expect.

The coefficients on the regression looks a bit odd. The three intercepts (95% interval in parenthesis) are -0.93 (-43.71 to 32.93), 0.85 (-16.23 to 26.47), 4.94 (-38.02 to 62.57). All the Rhat values are ~1.01, and the effective number of samples > 100, after 500 iterations across 3 chains. I might let it run a bit longer, just to see if it actually hasn’t converged yet.

I tried adding some structure to pull in the coefficients a bit by adding hyper priors, but it only helped slightly, though they were just uniform priors in the range 0-5. Reading through some of Gelman’s older work and searching on Google, I couldn’t really see if there are any recommendations for hyperpriors on regression coefficients.

Cheers,
David

messages.body_plain:
Let me try to be a little clearer.

  count: 7   outcome 1:  group 1
  count: 1   outcome 2:  group 1
  count: 3   outcome 1: group 2
  ...

That is, 7 times, items belonging to group 1 had outcome 1 and
1 time they had outcome 2.  For instance, the groupings might
be income and the outcomes votes for republican, democrat, or other.

You can then code this up as a multinomial, which in pseudocode is

  (7,1,0) ~ multinomial(theta[1]);

where theta[1] is the simplex of predictions for group 1.  Of course,
you'll need to build the array (7, 1, 0) --- you can't literally use
that notation in Stan yet.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable [cut points]
messages.body_plain:
Looks like nobody responded.

I think scaling a Dirichlet draw makes sense if you want to put
a prior that favors even distribution of segments.  I don't have
any intuition at all about how these problems work.

You have to be careful about what's getting sampled.  I wasn't
sure where that was in what you did.  This would work, with a
lower bound, width, and simplex parameters, combined into a
vector c of cutpoints.

parameters {
  real low;
  real width;
  simplex[K - 1] theta;
}
transformed parameters {
  ordered[K] c;
  c[0] <- low;
  for (i in 2:K)
    c[i] <- c[i - 1] + width * theta[k];
}
model {
  theta ~ dirichlet(rep(alpha, K - 1));
  low ~ ???
  width ~ ???

Why did you center yours on zero?  I'm also not sure about what
to do with the lower bound.  You need to make sure not to have
too many degress of freedom --- maybe the lower bound needs to
be fixed at theta?

I find it easier working directly in terms of a width parameter
rather than a half-width, but a lot of this is just personal preference.

- Bob

> On Sep 2, 2015, at 3:04 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
>
> Anyone care to comment on this possible prior for the effects of a K-level ordinal input variable? The idea is that you use a Dirichlet distribution for partitioning the range from beta[1] to beta[K], and you use an independent prior on the magnitude of that range.
>
>     beta[1] <- -scale;
>     beta[K] <- scale;
>     // Now make beta[k + 1] - beta[k] be fraction p[k] of (beta[K] - beta[1])
>     range <- beta[K] - beta[1];
>     b <- beta[1];
>     for (k = 1; k + 1 < K; ++k)
>         beta[k + 1] <- beta[k] + p[k] * range;
>
>     scale ~ normal(0, sigma);
>     p ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K-1));
>
> Larger values for alpha give a larger preference for equally-spaced betas.
>
> On Friday, August 28, 2015 at 1:30:44 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> This has been discussed before, albeit inconclusively.
>
> Yes, that's one way to do it.  I've been asking Andrew about this
> for a while and he didn't have a recommendation (or if he did, maybe
> he can remind us all).
>
> To construct a sequence of cutpoints, you can fix the first
> at 0 and then define
>
>   c[1] <- 0;
>   c[n+1] = c[n] + delta[n]
>
> where delta[n] has to be positive.  You can define
>
>  delta_raw ~ normal(0, 2);
>
> or another unconstrained prior and then take
>
>  delta <- exp(delta_raw);
>
> or you can constrain the delta to be positive and put any prior
> on them.  Like a lognormal or gamma.
>
> Or you can just model all the cutpoints as having independent
> priors, which gives you the same result as generating them
> independently and sorting given the constraint (I've verified this
> all computationally but haven't quite got my head around why it's
> true theoretically --- there are lots of moving boundaries to adjust
> for).
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> > On Aug 26, 2015, at 2:17 PM, Kevin Van Horn <ke...@ksvanhorn.com> wrote:
> >
> > I expressed that badly. What I actually had in mind was penalizing differences that are very small compared to beta[K] - beta[1] -- that is, although I don't want to assume equal spacing, I also consider something like -1, 0, 0.01, 1.3, where the effects for levels 2 and 3 are bunched up together, to be implausible.
> >
> > On Wednesday, August 26, 2015 at 12:08:03 PM UTC-6, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > No but that sounds like a funny prior---like anti-shrinkage on the differences.  I'd be interested in suggestions too.
> >
> > On Wednesday, August 26, 2015 at 1:59:21 PM UTC-4, Kevin Van Horn wrote:
> > Does anyone know of any literature on priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable? Here's what I have in mind:
> >         • You have an ordinal input variable x[N] with K levels.
> >         • You have K (or K-1) corresponding effects betax[K].
> >         • You must have betax[k+1] > betax[k].
> >         • The linear predictor for observation i includes a term betax[x[i]].
> > I don't want to have to assume that the betax values are equally spaced, but it would be good if the prior could penalize very small differences between beta[k] and beta[k+1].

messages.body_plain:
Shouldn't this be

y ~ poisson(alpha);
for(i in 1:n){
    increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-alpha[i]));
}
??

According to p109 of the manual, the PDF should be
p(y | lambda) = Poisson(y | lambda) / (1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
so log p = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
 = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - exp(-lambda)
 = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log1m_exp(-lambda)

OK. Re-reading your comments a few times, I think I finally understood it and managed to implement it as a model.

I restructured the data to be in the format,

count_outcome1, count_outcome2, count_outcome3, count_group, age_i, age_j, gender

So I can feed it directly into the model as,

(count_outcome1, count_outcome2, count_outcome3) ~ multinomial(softmax(b0 + b_age_i + b_age_j + b_gender))

the full model is at https://gist.github.com/demodw/248b2b7bcef06c82d741

When I run the model and re-generate the number of counts per outcome in the generated quantities block, it matches very closely what I am actually observing, so it seems like it is working. The coefficient estimate are, however, still very odd. In many cases the 95% HDI range from -50 +- 10 to 50 +- 10. I am not quite sure why. It seems like the model has converged (all Rhat < 1.1), though some variables have a low number of effective samples (<20). But even for variables with a large number of effective samples (>150) and Rhat < 1.01, the estimates are very broad. I tried putting uniform hyper priors on the priors of the coefficients, but even that did not help much. I am, however, wondering if the uniform is appropriate for that, or if there are other go-to hyper priors. Any advice on this one?

David

messages.body_plain:
I don't think that's going to work because you're trying to
fit a location theta[i] and a scale sigma_epsilon[i]
with only the single observation BP[i].

I think you need to fit the measurement error as something like this:

  BP[i] ~ normal(theta[i], sigma_BP);

where there is only a single scalar parameter sigma_BP for the
measurement errors.

Then, you can define a derived quantity for the error if you need
it, or put it in generated quantities or just calculate it on the
outside:

  transformed parameters {
    vector[I] err;
    err <- theta - BP;
  }

There's a chapter in the manual on coding measurement error models.

- Bob

Bob,

Sorry, I accidentally hit enter on Google Groups and then edited it after.  I assume you're getting this through the mailing list, so didn't see the edit.  What I wrote was this:
-----

y ~ poisson(alpha);
for(i in 1:n){

    increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-alpha[i]));

}
??

According to p109 of the manual, the PDF should be
p(y | lambda) = Poisson(y | lambda) / (1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
so log p = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
 = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - exp(-lambda)
 = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log1m_exp(-lambda)

----

messages.body_plain:
Clever --- I hadn't thought to reduce poisson_log(0, lambda)
further.  It inverts the "zeroes trick" from JAGS. :-)

I'll add a note that you can keep going on the reduction to the manual
and thank you for pointing it out:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617#issuecomment-144304649

- Bob

> On Sep 30, 2015, at 1:41 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob,
>
> Sorry, I accidentally hit enter on Google Groups and then edited it after.  I assume you're getting this through the mailing list, so didn't see the edit.  What I wrote was this:
> -----
> y ~ poisson(alpha);
> for(i in 1:n){
>     increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-alpha[i]));
> }
> ??
>
> According to p109 of the manual, the PDF should be
> p(y | lambda) = Poisson(y | lambda) / (1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
> so log p = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
>  = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - exp(-lambda)
>  = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log1m_exp(-lambda)
> ----
>
>
>
>
> On Wednesday, 30 September 2015 04:44:59 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> ???  There's nothing in the brackets.  Did something get lost in translation?
> You don't need brackets around a single statement if that's what you're worried
> about.
>
> I think what I wrote below is OK assuming alpha's computed ahead of time
> as a vector.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
> > On Sep 29, 2015, at 7:42 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Shouldn't this be
> >
> > y ~ poisson(alpha);
> > for(i in 1:n){
> >
> > }
> >
> > On Tuesday, 29 September 2015 03:40:46 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> > Alternatively, you can do the simple case of the Poisson by realizing
> > that the relevant CDF (1 - poisson_cdf(1, alpha[n])) can be coded
> > as (1 - exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n])).  Because you're going to need
> > that on the log scale, and it's a common operation, we have it built in
> > as
> >
> >   log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]);
> >
> > So you could code the whole model as
> >
> >   y ~ poisson(alpha);
> >   for (n in 1:N)
> >     increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]));
> >
> > Considerably uglier.  Now if the alpha[n] were all the same, it
> > could be made much more efficient.  As is, allowing the vectorization
> > now in the Poisson sampling statement shouldn't be too bad.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > > On Sep 28, 2015, at 4:16 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > An update on this:
> > >
> > >         • I tried a negative binomial model, then just moved back to plain Poisson because the overdispersion in the data is not material
