> > >         • I am using a dense mass matrix and this helps, I think
> > >         • I have used adapt_delta = 0.9, and this seems to help
> > >         • Looking at the posterior for coefficients of the simplex regressor groups reveals very high correlations (r > 0.9), so this isn't exactly a very easy posterior to sample from.  Somewhat informative priors seem to have helped here, as per the suggestion in the manual for nearly-unidentified parameters.
> > >         • It seems that simply a lot of warmup iterations are needed in order for Stan to learn the shape of the posterior.  With n=500 warmup iterations, max_treedepth is hit on most iterations early on, and progressively less later.  With larger numbers of warmup iterations the average number of leapfrog steps seems to decline, but there doesn't appear to be a 'eureka' moment where suddenly sampling quality drastically improves.
> > >
> > > Unfortunately it just looks like I have a slow model.  My data re are constructed so that y=0 never appears, so I have to use a ~ poisson T[1,] statement, which is unfortunately not vectorised.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I'm happy that the model is working as intended, and the run time is long but not unmanageably.   Thanks for your help.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Monday, 28 September 2015 15:44:54 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > >

> > > > Thanks Bob - much appreciated.
> > > >

> > > >
> > > > I guess that this is the source of the problem. I will try rescaling my inputs so that the likely posterior has a much more uniform scale over the different variables.
> > >
> > > That should help considerably.
> > >
> > > > Thanks once again for your help guys - I realise how busy you are and how many requests you get and am grateful for your assistance.
> > >
> > > You're welcome.  Problems like this one are good because
> > > we need to diagnose how Stan can fail.  Ideally, we'd like to
> > > improve our adaptation routines as well as our diagnostics.
> > >

messages.subject: Syntax highlighting for Stan models in LaTeX
messages.subject_clean: Syntax highlighting for Stan models in LaTeX
messages.body_plain:
I just wanted to let people know about a few tools for syntax highlighting Stan models typeset in LaTeX.

lstbayes is a LaTeX package that provides Stan language support for the listings <https://www.ctan.org/pkg/listings?lang=en> package, which provides environments to highlight code in LaTeX. lstbayes just went up on CTAN (https://www.ctan.org/pkg/lstbayes), so you'll have to install it manually from either CTAN or github (https://github.com/jrnold/lstbayes). See https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/LaTeX/Installing_Extra_Packages if you've never manually installed a LaTeX package. Though, with lstbayes, all you really need to do is put lstbayes.sty in the same directory as your .tex file.

Additionally Pygments <http://pygments.org/> has support for python, e.g. http://pygments.org/demo/2784566/. If you haven't stumbled across it, Pygments is a python package and command line tool that is generic code highlighter that outputs to a variety of format including LaTeX and HTML. You can easily use it to highlight code chunks within LaTeX using the minted <https://github.com/gpoore/minted> package.

Hope these are of some use.

messages.body_plain:
Just to provide a further update on my general problem:

I have not been able to materially speed up the model (iterations per second) through simply recoding the Poisson calculation
I continued to struggle with convergence issues, until I standardised every regressor to have mean zero and standard deviation 1.  This has made a massive improvement to the model, I suspect by reducing posterior correlations (I have interaction terms as well, which behave oddly unless standardised).  I had some concerns about this given the simplex-like nature of blocks of my regressors, but in fact this seems to be fine.
I have had to use adapt_delta = 0.9 in order to minimise the number of divergent transitions
I have increased max_treedepth to 11, but still hit up against the max_treedepth quite often.

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the parameter correlations are very high given the simplex constraint.  I have a Gaussian shrinkage prior on every parameter to try to deal with the problem, so the prior is nominally proper, but appreciate that it can take a long time to explore.

With the shrinkage prior, the posterior is not entirely elliptical, which adds to the problem.

Warmup of 1,000 to 2,000 iterations seems to produce reasonable results thereafter (although with about one effective sample per 10-20 iterations).  It's not slow, but thankfully I can run a large number of chains in parallel, so it's not intolerable to get a good level of accuracy.  It makes debugging a pain though.

Thanks for the comment.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Log Gaussian Cox Process Model in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Log Gaussian Cox Process Model in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Beth. For a few thousand grid cells, I think that it'll eventually
get to the point that Stan can handle it, but it's not there yet.
It'll probably take Riemannian HMC (which should come at some point,
don't know the timeline) and some more work on dedicated matrix
algebra operations, e.g. some of the ones detailed here:
https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/60

I guess it depends on your timeline, i.e. if you need an answer
immediately, I'd try INLA (or GPstuff or GPy). But I certainly think
it'd be instructive to give it a go now in Stan, and try ADVI. Some
Stan code that might be helpful is at the end of my manuscript that's
in preparation, here's a link:
http://sethrf.com/files/fast-hierarchical-GPs.pdf

Seth

On Wed, Sep 30, 2015 at 3:12 AM, Ziniti Beth Louise

<roberts.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you to everyone for the helpful comments!
>
> Michael Betancourt, you mention that Euclidean HMC has a difficult time with
> LGCP. Is Riemann HMC better? and if so, is or will it be implemented in
> Stan?
>
> Seth Flaxman, thank you for your paper reference! I have considered the grid
> approach as Diggle et al (2013) describes along with his r package LGCP. The
> only other alternative I had been aware of is INLA (Rue et al. 2009). My
> application window size is maybe moderate, a couple thousand grid cells.
>
> --Beth
>
> On Friday, September 25, 2015 at 7:00:36 AM UTC-4, Seth Flaxman wrote:
>>
>> Hi. I am very interested in getting this to work. The closest I'm aware of
>> is probably the Kronecker GP stuff I've been working on--if you're happy
>> with gridding up your counts, you can approximate an LGCP with a GP with
>> Poisson observation model and use Kronecker (or FFT) for scalability [see my
>> ICML paper, not Stan though]--but I did indeed run into issues with the non
>> Gaussian observation model in Stan. Happy to share code in any case... And
>> also this was before ADVI was around so that might help!
>>
>> What's the scale of your data / observation window? Had you thought about
>> how you'd like to set it up, e.g. using a grid as I did (following Diggle et
>> al), or more like the sigmoidal idea [Adams 2009] or uniformization [Teh
>> 2011]. I haven't thought yet about how we might implement those in Stan, but
>> I'd be happy to discuss more.

messages.body_plain:
There is no “true latent variable”.  Because you don’t measure the latent variable
directly you’ll always be uncertain about it and hence have some mixture of 0 and 1,
which is what q tells you directly.  If you want to remove outliers you can now do
something well posed, like construct a loss function and choose the option that
minimizes expected loss.  Or just take z = 1 if  q > 0.5 and z = 0 otherwise.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Poisson regression model very slow - because of simplex groups of regressors?
messages.body_plain:
Might it be possible to fix this by going to a (K-1)-factor
basis for the simplex rather than a K-factor basis?  We need more
discussion of this issue in the manual.  Our K-simplex parameters
in Stan are parameterized in the unconstrained space with (K-1) free
parameters.

- Bob

> On Sep 30, 2015, at 5:38 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Yes, the parameter correlations are very high given the simplex constraint.  I have a Gaussian shrinkage prior on every parameter to try to deal with the problem, so the prior is nominally proper, but appreciate that it can take a long time to explore.
>
> With the shrinkage prior, the posterior is not entirely elliptical, which adds to the problem.
>
> Warmup of 1,000 to 2,000 iterations seems to produce reasonable results thereafter (although with about one effective sample per 10-20 iterations).  It's not slow, but thankfully I can run a large number of chains in parallel, so it's not intolerable to get a good level of accuracy.  It makes debugging a pain though.
>
> Thanks for the comment.
>
>
> On Wednesday, 30 September 2015 18:38:55 UTC+10, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Have you plotting the parameter correlations? This sounds a lot like non-identifiability (your posterior is concentrating
> on a warped cigar, which requires very small step sizes and long integration times to explore) which isn’t surprising given
> the simplex constraint.
>
> On Sep 30, 2015, at 9:34 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Just to provide a further update on my general problem:
>>
>> 	• I have not been able to materially speed up the model (iterations per second) through simply recoding the Poisson calculation
>> 	• I continued to struggle with convergence issues, until I standardised every regressor to have mean zero and standard deviation 1.  This has made a massive improvement to the model, I suspect by reducing posterior correlations (I have interaction terms as well, which behave oddly unless standardised).  I had some concerns about this given the simplex-like nature of blocks of my regressors, but in fact this seems to be fine.
>> 	• I have had to use adapt_delta = 0.9 in order to minimise the number of divergent transitions
>> 	• I have increased max_treedepth to 11, but still hit up against the max_treedepth quite often.
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Wednesday, 30 September 2015 17:02:06 UTC+10, Julian King wrote:
>> No problems.  Not sure how it affects the vectorisation and so whether there is any significant speed difference.  Obviously if lambda is the same everywhere you can make it common, but in a Poisson regression model it's not.
>>
>>
>> On Wednesday, 30 September 2015 16:49:38 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Clever --- I hadn't thought to reduce poisson_log(0, lambda)
>> further.  It inverts the "zeroes trick" from JAGS. :-)
>>
>> I'll add a note that you can keep going on the reduction to the manual
>> and thank you for pointing it out:
>>
>> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617#issuecomment-144304649
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> > On Sep 30, 2015, at 1:41 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >
>> > Bob,
>> >
>> > Sorry, I accidentally hit enter on Google Groups and then edited it after.  I assume you're getting this through the mailing list, so didn't see the edit.  What I wrote was this:
>> > -----
>> > y ~ poisson(alpha);
>> > for(i in 1:n){
>> >     increment_log_prob(-log1m_exp(-alpha[i]));
>> > }
>> > ??
>> >
>> > According to p109 of the manual, the PDF should be
>> > p(y | lambda) = Poisson(y | lambda) / (1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
>> > so log p = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - PoissonCDF(0 | lambda))
>> >  = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log(1 - exp(-lambda)
>> >  = log_Poisson(y | lambda) - log1m_exp(-lambda)
>> > ----
>> >
>> >
>> >
>> >
>> > On Wednesday, 30 September 2015 04:44:59 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> > ???  There's nothing in the brackets.  Did something get lost in translation?
>> > You don't need brackets around a single statement if that's what you're worried
>> > about.
>> >
>> > I think what I wrote below is OK assuming alpha's computed ahead of time
>> > as a vector.
>> >
>> > - Bob
>> >
>> >
>> >
>> > > On Sep 29, 2015, at 7:42 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > >
>> > > Shouldn't this be
>> > >
>> > > y ~ poisson(alpha);
>> > > for(i in 1:n){
>> > >
>> > > }
>> > >
>> > > On Tuesday, 29 September 2015 03:40:46 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> > >
>> > > Alternatively, you can do the simple case of the Poisson by realizing
>> > > that the relevant CDF (1 - poisson_cdf(1, alpha[n])) can be coded
>> > > as (1 - exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n])).  Because you're going to need
>> > > that on the log scale, and it's a common operation, we have it built in
>> > > as
>> > >
>> > >   log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]);
>> > >
>> > > So you could code the whole model as
>> > >
>> > >   y ~ poisson(alpha);
>> > >   for (n in 1:N)
>> > >     increment_log_prob(log1m_exp(poisson_log(0, alpha[n]));
>> > >
>> > > Considerably uglier.  Now if the alpha[n] were all the same, it
>> > > could be made much more efficient.  As is, allowing the vectorization
>> > > now in the Poisson sampling statement shouldn't be too bad.
>> > >
>> > > - Bob
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > >
>> > > > On Sep 28, 2015, at 4:16 AM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > > >
>> > > > An update on this:
>> > > >
>> > > >         • I tried a negative binomial model, then just moved back to plain Poisson because the overdispersion in the data is not material
>> > > >         • Placing somewhat more informative (but still pretty vague) priors seems to have helped
>> > > >         • I am using a dense mass matrix and this helps, I think
>> > > >         • I have used adapt_delta = 0.9, and this seems to help
>> > > >         • Looking at the posterior for coefficients of the simplex regressor groups reveals very high correlations (r > 0.9), so this isn't exactly a very easy posterior to sample from.  Somewhat informative priors seem to have helped here, as per the suggestion in the manual for nearly-unidentified parameters.
>> > > >         • It seems that simply a lot of warmup iterations are needed in order for Stan to learn the shape of the posterior.  With n=500 warmup iterations, max_treedepth is hit on most iterations early on, and progressively less later.  With larger numbers of warmup iterations the average number of leapfrog steps seems to decline, but there doesn't appear to be a 'eureka' moment where suddenly sampling quality drastically improves.
>> > > >
>> > > > Unfortunately it just looks like I have a slow model.  My data re are constructed so that y=0 never appears, so I have to use a ~ poisson T[1,] statement, which is unfortunately not vectorised.
>> > > >
>> > > >
>> > > >
>> > > > I'm happy that the model is working as intended, and the run time is long but not unmanageably.   Thanks for your help.
>> > > >
>> > > >
>> > > >
>> > > >
>> > > > On Monday, 28 September 2015 15:44:54 UTC+10, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> > > >
>> > > > > On Sep 26, 2015, at 8:50 PM, Julian King <jking...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> > > > >
>> > > > > Thanks Bob - much appreciated.
>> > > > >
>> > > > > The suggestion to look at the mass matrix was a good one. The inverse diagonal weights reported range from ~1e-6 to ~10. Looking at the posterior summary outputs, it turns out that some of my parameters are just much better constrained in the regression than others.
>> > > > >
>> > > > > I guess that this is the source of the problem. I will try rescaling my inputs so that the likely posterior has a much more uniform scale over the different variables.
>> > > >
>> > > > That should help considerably.
>> > > >
>> > > > > Thanks once again for your help guys - I realise how busy you are and how many requests you get and am grateful for your assistance.
>> > > >
>> > > > You're welcome.  Problems like this one are good because
>> > > > we need to diagnose how Stan can fail.  Ideally, we'd like to
>> > > > improve our adaptation routines as well as our diagnostics.
>> > > >
>> > > > > Is there any way to pass in an initial guess at the mass matrix? Or is this for a future release?  Being able to specify guessed scales for the parameters would be more convenient in some applications than having to recode parameters.
>> > > >
>> > > > Not right now, but there will be in the future.  It's
>> > > > part of the Stan 3 refactor of the API between the
>> > > > interfaces (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan) and the language.
>> > > > I'm not forgetting the other interfaces, but they all
>> > > > call CmdStan, so should be insulated from these changes.
>> > > >
>> > > > - Bob

While I really like the declarative model building in Stan, it had me thinking about the problem in the wrong way.  I've enjoyed the philosophical discussion, and some of the comments spurred me to look at the problem a bit differently.  I think I've figured out what I need to do to move forward (but alas it involves writing my own MCMC code rather than using Stan).  Thanks, all!

messages.body_plain:
I still don't think Stan is "declarative" in any useful
sense.  It uses imperative programming constructs (loops,
conditionals, local variables, etc.), and uses them to define
a log density, which it can then sample from.  That's really
all Stan's doing.

If you want to sample from that model using custom MCMC code,
you'll still need to be careful with the constraints on the
x parameters imposed by your model:

  y[i] ~ lognormal(log(a[i, 1] * x[i, 1] + a[i, 2] * x[i, 2] + a[i, 3] * x[i, 3]), epsilon);

And you still need to respect any required Jacobians, because
that's just probability theory.   If the a > 0 and the x > 0
by construction, there shouldn't be a problem fitting this in Stan.

Good luck!

- Bob
